findings.topic: AI personas on finance topics
findings.official_quote: This includes any content that presents itself as a human expert providing advice to viewers on topics such as health, legal issues, finances, or politics. To protect viewers who may be confused or otherwise negatively impacted by this content, channels uploading this content will not be allowed to monetize.
findings.applies: This is the only YouTube rule I found that names finance. YouTube's example of what breaks it is "AI-generated podcast hosts offering financial guidance, investment tips, or wealth management advice". The penalty covers the whole channel ("channels uploading this content"). The kit as written does not break it. The description says it is for education only and that no video says what to buy or sell. Sam is a drawn character in a story, not a presenter. The script calls the 7% "made-up" and says it "isn't a promise about any investment". The risk is in how the videos get voiced and how future scripts drift. findings.topic: Inauthentic (templated) content
findings.official_quote: That means channels where content feels interchangeable from video to video are not allowed to monetize. In other words, your channel shouldn’t have content that appears to be produced using a template or where each video doesn’t deliver creative, educational, or other value to the viewer.
findings.applies: A stick-figure explainer channel is the format most exposed to this rule: same characters, same canvas, same narration rhythm. YouTube allows "Similar content, like a series following a set of characters across episodes or a channel that does product reviews, but in which each video has a distinct storyline, focus, or concept". It refuses "Videos where characters are put in the same situation over and over again with the same outcome (i.e., using a highly similar storyline template across multiple videos)". Video 1 compares two copies of Sam side by side, and title 6 already plans the same two-figure comparison and names the format rather than the idea. Reviewers look at the channel's main theme, newest videos, titles and About section. The reused-content rule also refuses "Content that exclusively features readings of other materials you did not originally create, like text from websites or news feeds", so a script adapted from an explainer site would fail.
findings.action: Give each video its own visual idea and structure, so the side-by-side comparison isn't the default, and write every script yourself from sources. Before uploading, watch the last three videos in a row and change anything that feels interchangeable. It also helps reviewers if the About text says, truthfully, that the scripts and drawings are made for this channel.

findings.topic: AI mass-production (Spam policy)
findings.official_quote: Using automated tools or AI to churn out high volumes of similar content with minimal changes. While testing out new creation tools or posting a few variations of a video is ok, we don't allow use of these tools to flood our platform with repetitive content.
findings.applies: This is a Community Guidelines rule, not just a monetization one: "If your content violates this policy, we may suspend your monetization or terminate your channel or account." YouTube's own example is the faceless-explainer shape: "Example: Channels that use the exact same background music and repetitive AI generated imagery across many videos, with each video reading out an AI-generated script." A drawn money channel voiced by AI and scripted by AI, uploaded at volume, would match that example closely.
findings.action: Upload only as fast as you can write and check each video by hand, and vary the music. If AI helps with scripts, use it the way YouTube lists as allowed ("using AI to edit your video scripts"), not to write whole scripts.

findings.topic: Made for kids setting
findings.official_quote: Whether the video includes characters, celebrities, or toys that appeal to children, including animated characters or cartoon figures.
findings.applies: Stick figures and plain words are two of the kid-appeal factors YouTube lists, so this channel is more exposed than a talking-head finance channel. The subjects (loans, credit scores, taxes, recessions) make it general audience. YouTube's general-audience examples include "Animated content that appeals to everyone", and it says a video is not made for kids just because "It’s safe or appropriate for everyone to watch (aka it’s “family friendly”)." The page also says the creator is legally responsible under COPPA for setting this correctly.
findings.action: In YouTube Studio, set the channel to "No, set this channel as not made for kids. I almost never upload content that’s made for kids." Keep kid-targeting signals out of titles, tags and visuals: no "for kids", no school-age framing, no nursery-style songs or toys.

findings.topic: AI disclosure (voice and real people)
findings.official_quote: Creators don’t need to disclose non-realistic content that’s made with AI, or edits to realistic content that are minor.
findings.applies: Stick-figure drawings are not realistic, so AI help with them needs no label. "Cloning one’s own voice to create voice overs or dubs" is on the no-disclosure list. The page's test is whether content "seems realistic", and its lists don't say either way whether an invented AI narrator voice needs a label. The money videos will mention central bankers and well-known investors, for example in the recession and money-creation videos. Disclosure is required for content that "Makes a real person appear to say or do something they didn’t do." One of YouTube's must-disclose examples is "Making it appear as if someone gave advice that they did not actually give". YouTube also says: "Note: Disclosing AI content alone won’t limit a video’s audience or impact its eligibility to earn money."
findings.action: Answer "AI use" in Studio's Attributes on every upload. Choose No for drawn videos narrated by you or your own cloned voice. Choose Yes for any realistic AI footage or audio, and if unsure about an AI voice, choose Yes. Never generate the voice or likeness of a real economist, central banker or investor: show their words as on-screen text with a source.

findings.official_quote: Scams: Promoting "get rich quick" investment schemes, fake job offers, or sharing fake "customer support" contact information to steal private data like bank details, passwords, or government IDs.

The policy "applies to all types of content on YouTube, including unlisted and private content, comments, links, posts and thumbnails". The kit passes. Three strikes here would also put the owner's other linked channels at risk.
findings.action: Use only archive images and footage that are licensed, made for the channel, or clearly in the public domain, and keep a short record for each video: source, licence, date. If a takedown arrives, remove or replace the material rather than disputing it without a real basis, then complete Copyright School so the strike expires after 90 days.

findings.topic: Reused content (news clips and archive material)
findings.official_quote: Reused content refers to channels that repurpose content that’s already on YouTube or another online source without adding significant original commentary, substantive modifications, or educational or entertainment value. … Our reused content policy applies to your channel as a whole. If you have videos that violate our guidelines, or if we cannot clearly tell that you made the content, monetization may be removed from your entire channel.
findings.applies: A faceless documentary channel made from news clips and archive photos is exactly what this policy checks. It is judged across the whole channel. The same page says reviewers read the 'Channel description' to see how the content was made, and it lists "Reused content from other online sources where the creator is either visible in the content or explains how the creator added to the content" as allowed. It also lists "Content that exclusively features readings of other materials you did not originally create, like text from websites or news feeds" as not allowed. The kit's description says where the facts come from, but not what the channel makes itself.
findings.action: Each film must be mainly the channel's own writing, narration, charts and illustrations. Third-party clips should be short evidence that the narration discusses, never a run of news clips with reporting read over them. Say in the description how the films are made, and only say what is true.

kit_edit.quote: Every date and figure comes from public records, filings and reporting, listed under each video.
kit_edit.replace_with: Every film is researched and written for this channel, with charts and illustrations made for it. Every date and figure comes from public records, filings and reporting, listed under each video with credits for any archive images.

findings.topic: AI images of real people and events
findings.official_quote: Creators must disclose GenAI content that: • Makes a real person appear to say or do something they didn’t do. • Alters footage of a real event or place. • Generates a realistic scene that didn’t actually occur. … Creators who consistently choose not to disclose this information may be subject to manual application of a label, or penalties from YouTube, including removal of content or suspension from the YouTube Partner Program.
findings.applies: The script calls for an "Archive-style still of the prototype" and a "Boardroom illustration" of Kodak's managers reacting. If either is made to look like a real photo with AI, it shows real people and a real moment as they never were, and it needs the AI label. An AI image made to pass as a 1970s archive photo also runs into the monetization policy's "Content that uses deceptive or misleading imagery or narratives" (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/1311392). Drawings that are plainly drawings need no label, and neither does AI help with the script or infographics ("Production assistance, like using generative AI tools to create or improve a video outline, script, thumbnail, title, or infographic").
findings.action: Show the prototype with a drawing made for the film, or with Kodak's real photo used with permission and credited. Never use an AI fake made to look like an archive photo. Keep the boardroom scene plainly drawn. If any realistic AI image of a real person or event is used, set 'AI use' to Yes in Studio when uploading. Never make a real executive's voice or face with AI.

kit_edit.quote: [Archive-style still of the prototype]
kit_edit.replace_with: [Drawing of the prototype, made for this film (or Kodak's own photo, licensed and credited)]

findings.topic: Defamation: real companies and living people
findings.official_quote: Defamation laws vary by country but usually concern content that damages the reputation of another person or business. Although the definition of defamation varies around the world, in general, defamation is any untrue statement that is harmful to someone's reputation or causes someone to be shunned or avoided. … If you choose to pursue legal action against the content creator, note that we may be prepared to comply with any order requiring the content creator to remove the posting in question.
findings.applies: Most of the companies still exist (Kodak, Nokia, BlackBerry, LEGO, the Toys "R" Us brand) and many insiders are alive. YouTube's complaint form covers "The exact statements in the video or metadata that you allege are defamatory" (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/6154216), so titles count as well as narration. Title 1 says Kodak "Hid It", but the same script ends on "the patents Kodak held", and a patent is a public filing, so "hid" goes further than the script itself supports. The script also puts "Keep it quiet." on screen in quotation marks, as if managers said those words. The risk is low because YouTube does not remove videos on an allegation alone, but titles stay up for years.
findings.action: Retitle the Kodak film and change scriptTitle to match. Put words in quotation marks only when someone is reported to have said them, and say who. Third-party reports of a New York Times interview give Sasson's memory of management's reaction as "that's cute — but don't tell anyone about it"; check the original before quoting it. Say whose account a disputed story is. For example, Blockbuster 'laughing' comes from the Netflix side, so attribute it in the video.

kit_edit.quote: Kodak Invented the Digital Camera. Then Hid It.
kit_edit.replace_with: Kodak Invented the Digital Camera. Then Shelved It.

findings.topic: Made for kids (LEGO and Toys "R" Us films)
findings.official_quote: General audience content is content that could appeal to everyone, but isn’t intended specifically for children, or content that is intended for a teen or older audience. General audience content should be set as “not made for kids.” … Just because your content may include some of these factors does not automatically mean it’s made for kids.
findings.applies: The channel covers bankruptcies, a financial crisis and layoffs, for adults. The LEGO and Toys "R" Us films will show toys, and YouTube lists "Whether the video includes characters, celebrities, or toys that appeal to children" as a factor. A factor alone does not make a film made for kids, but childlike packaging could tip it.
findings.action: In Studio, set the channel default to 'No, it's not made for kids' and check it on every upload. For LEGO and Toys "R" Us, frame thumbnails and titles around the business story, not bright toy-play images or children's language, and never aim tags or promotion at children.

findings.topic: Fair use: credit is not permission
findings.official_quote: Giving credit to the owner of a copyrighted work won’t by itself turn a non-transformative copy of their material into fair use. Phrases like “all rights go to the author” and “I do not own” don’t automatically mean you’re making fair use of that material. … The claim will keep you from monetizing the video, even if you only use a few seconds, such as short uses of popular songs.
findings.applies: The description's promise to list sources is right for facts. But a source list or a 'footage courtesy of' line does not license a photo or clip. Old Kodak, Polaroid and Blockbuster adverts (often with music), press photos and news coverage of Lehman are the material most likely to be claimed, and a single claim takes that video's ad money.
findings.action: For each piece of someone else's material: license it, or use only a short part that the narration is analysing on screen. If it would only be decoration, replace it with a chart, map or drawing. Take music only from the YouTube Audio Library or a licence that covers YouTube, never from old adverts or newscasts. Don't rely on 'no copyright intended' lines.

findings.topic: Company logos and trademarks
findings.official_quote: Trademark infringement is improper or unauthorized use of a trademark in a way that is likely to cause confusion as to the source of that product. YouTube policies prohibit videos and channels that infringe trademarks. If your content uses someone else’s trademarks in a way that might cause confusion, your videos can be blocked. Your channel may also be suspended.
findings.applies: Showing the Kodak, Nokia or Blockbuster logo to name a film's subject is not the problem. The problem is anything that suggests the company made or approved the channel: a logo as the avatar or banner, a brand in the handle, or thumbnails styled like the company's own adverts. The impersonation policy (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2801947) adds: "Impersonation may include deceptively copying the branding, content, or usernames of individuals, channels or entities."
findings.action: Keep company logos and brand names out of the channel name, handle, avatar and banner. In thumbnails, use a logo only as a small identifier inside the channel's own design. Say in the description that the channel is not connected to the companies it covers.

kit_edit.quote: These are stories, not advice. Nothing here is a recommendation to invest in anything.
kit_edit.replace_with: These are stories, not advice. Nothing here is a recommendation to invest in anything, and this channel isn't connected to or endorsed by any company it covers.

findings.topic: Naming living people; employees in archive photos
findings.official_quote: We aim to protect your privacy while balancing public interest and newsworthiness. … We also consider public interest, newsworthiness, consent, and whether the information is otherwise publicly available. … A first name without additional context, or a fleeting image, would not likely qualify as uniquely identifiable.
findings.applies: Executives and inventors such as Steven Sasson, Lehman's leaders and Blockbuster's and Netflix's bosses acted in public roles. The harassment policy explicitly allows "Content featuring debates or discussions of topical issues concerning individuals who have positions of power, like high-profile government officials or CEOs of major multinational corporations." (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2802268). Ordinary people in news photos are different: Lehman staff carrying boxes out, or laid-off Kodak and Toys "R" Us workers. They can file a privacy complaint if they can be identified. The same page also lists "Simulating audio to make it sound like a person is saying something they have not said" as a privacy violation.
findings.action: Name people only for what they did in their business or public role, from cited sources. Blur ordinary employees and bystanders who can be identified, or don't linger on them. Never show personal details, and never make a real person's voice or face with AI.

findings.topic: Tragedies inside company stories (Pan Am, 2008 crisis)
findings.official_quote: Content where the focal point is on blood, violence, or injury, when presented without other context, is not suitable for advertising. If you're showing violent content in a news, educational, artistic, or documentary context, that additional context is important. … Footage of disasters that involve visible harm to people or their resulting suffering, such as extreme emotional distress. … Our policies apply to all portions of your content (video, Short, or live stream, thumbnail, title, description, and tags).
findings.applies: Pan Am's story includes the Lockerbie bombing (1988) and the Tenerife collision (1977), and the Lehman film covers the 2008 crash. The same page lists "Educational, journalistic reports, or music videos discussing a terrorist attack as a central subject." as content that can earn ads. Disaster footage showing visible suffering is in the Violence section's group that earns limited ads, and the rules apply to thumbnails and titles too.
findings.action: Tell tragedies through narration and facts, using maps, timelines and non-graphic or memorial images. Use no wreckage-with-victims footage or shots of grieving families, and keep crashes and deaths out of thumbnails and titles. Give the context inside the video itself; the EDSA page says to "include the info in your video, not just your video’s title or description" (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/6345162).

findings.topic: Same story template every time (inauthentic content)
findings.official_quote: Videos where characters are put in the same situation over and over again with the same outcome (i.e., using a highly similar storyline template across multiple videos) … AI-generated content made with generic or unoriginal templates giving the impression of mass production without adding the creator’s original, authentic insights or perspective
findings.applies: The description promises the same arc every time ("from its best decision to its worst"), and most of the ten titles are rise-and-fall stories. YouTube still allows a series "in which each video has a distinct storyline, focus, or concept". But a fixed 'rise, mistake, collapse' script with the names swapped is what the July 15, 2025 'inauthentic content' update targets, and reviewers judge the whole channel.
findings.action: Build each film around its own question and its own evidence (Kodak: patents against film profits; LEGO: a comeback; Lehman: one weekend). Vary the structure and visuals, and don't produce scripts in batches from one template. Keep comebacks like LEGO in the mix.

findings.topic: AI narrator and money advice
findings.official_quote: This includes any content that presents itself as a human expert providing advice to viewers on topics such as health, legal issues, finances, or politics. To protect viewers who may be confused or otherwise negatively impacted by this content, channels uploading this content will not be allowed to monetize. … AI-generated podcast hosts offering financial guidance, investment tips, or wealth management advice
findings.applies: Stories about Lehman, bankruptcies and share prices invite 'lessons for investors' segments. If the narrator is an AI voice or AI presenter, that turns into this banned category. The kit's description already says "These are stories, not advice.", which is right.
findings.action: Keep the films as history. No stock picks, no 'what this means for your money', and no 'should you buy' titles, especially for companies that still trade (Nokia, BlackBerry, Kodak). If an AI voice narrates, never present it as a named human expert.

review.notes:
Every page was read with the official reader, and none returned COULD NOT READ. Every finding marked official quotes those pages word for word.

Caveats:
- The reader removes repeated lines, so in the advertiser-friendly guidelines the heading "This content will receive limited ad earnings" is printed only once. Placing the disaster-footage examples in that group is read from the page's order.
- Two facts in the defamation finding come from outside sources and are not YouTube rules: Sasson's "that's cute — but don't tell anyone about it" (reported from a New York Times interview) and Kodak's patent. For the patent, the script's own line "the patents Kodak held" is enough to make the point. The fact-check step should confirm both against the originals.
- The spam policy's "Malicious clickbait" rule (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2801973) needs no change. It just means each title must deliver its story: the Blockbuster film must actually cover that meeting, and "Why Toys "R" Us Really Closed" must give a reason backed by evidence.
- The channel name was ignored as asked. The script's closing line "This is Rise and Ruin Files" will change with the new name.
- Defamation and fair use are finally legal questions. YouTube says it does not judge them itself and will act on court orders or valid takedowns.

review.audience_setting: not made for kids: YouTube Help says "General audience content is content that could appeal to everyone, but isn’t intended specifically for children, or content that is intended for a teen or older audience. General audience content should be set as “not made for kids.”" These explainers are about phones, chatbots, search and batteries, written for the adults and teens who use them, not for under-13s.

findings.topic: Inauthentic content (generic, repetitive or mass-produced AI)
findings.official_quote: What’s important is that the substance of each video should be materially varied and deliver creative, educational, or other value. ... • Similar content, like a series following a set of characters across episodes or a channel that does product reviews, but in which each video has a distinct storyline, focus, or concept ... • AI-generated content made with generic or unoriginal templates giving the impression of mass production without adding the creator’s original, authentic insights or perspective
findings.applies: This is a faceless explainer channel that will probably use AI for scripts, visuals or voice, and it has a fixed format: an on-screen question, a simple animation, a one-line takeaway, then 'Next:'. A recurring format is allowed if each video has its own focus, and the first script passes: it builds an original worked example ('The cat sat on the ___') with real teaching value. The risk comes later, if videos start to feel interchangeable or batch-made from one AI template. Reviewers look at the channel's main theme, newest videos, metadata and About section, not single videos, and a failure blocks monetization for the whole channel.
findings.action: Give every video its own worked example and its own visuals, as the first script does. A shared intro and outro is fine. Never batch-generate scripts or visuals from one template: rewrite every AI draft in your own explanation before recording.

findings.topic: Disclosing AI-generated visuals (AI use setting)
findings.official_quote: We require creators to disclose AI-generated or altered content that seems realistic. ... Creators must disclose GenAI content that: • Makes a real person appear to say or do something they didn’t do. ... • Generates a realistic scene that didn’t actually occur. ... Creators don’t need to disclose non-realistic content that’s made with AI, or edits to realistic content that are minor. ... Production assistance, like using generative AI tools to create or improve a video outline, script, thumbnail, title, or infographic ... Note: Disclosing AI content alone won’t limit a video’s audience or impact its eligibility to earn money. ... Creators who consistently choose not to disclose this information may be subject to manual application of a label, or penalties from YouTube, including removal of content or suspension from the YouTube Partner Program.
findings.applies: Most videos need no disclosure. The first script uses diagrams, bars, a dice icon and boxes, which are non-realistic or infographic, and an AI-written script is production help. Two planned videos are exposed: 'How Image Generators Turn Noise Into Pictures' and probably 'Why AI Makes Things Up' will show sample AI output. A photorealistic AI image or clip of a scene that never happened counts as 'a realistic scene that didn’t actually occur', even inside an explainer. An AI image of a real person, such as a tech CEO, is the highest risk: it needs disclosure, and YouTube's privacy process lets that person ask for removal.
findings.action: For each upload, set YouTube Studio > Attributes > 'AI use'. Choose No for diagram-only videos. Choose Yes for any video that shows photorealistic AI images or video, and label those examples on screen as AI-made. Never use AI to show a real, identifiable person.

findings.topic: AI narration voice
findings.official_quote: Examples of content, edits, or video assistance that creators don’t need to disclose: ... • Cloning one’s own voice to create voice overs or dubs ... Labels may appear in the expanded description for non-music AI-generated audio or AI content that is non-photorealistic or animated.
findings.applies: A faceless channel has to choose a narrator. Your own voice, or an AI clone of your own voice, is explicitly exempt from disclosure. A stock, realistic AI voice that isn't yours is not settled by the current Help page. YouTube's March 2024 announcement (https://blog.youtube/news-and-events/disclosing-ai-generated-content/) listed it among the cases that need disclosure: 'Using the likeness of a realistic person: Digitally altering content to replace the face of one individual with another's or synthetically generating a person’s voice to narrate a video.' Using a voice that sounds like a real, identifiable person is clearly covered.
findings.action: Best: narrate in your own voice or a clone of it, which needs no disclosure. If you use a stock realistic AI voice, answer Yes to 'AI use'. It costs only a label in the description and doesn't affect reach or earnings. Never use a voice that imitates a real person.

findings.topic: Reused content (press footage, keynotes, read-aloud articles)
findings.official_quote: Reused content refers to channels that repurpose content that’s already on YouTube or another online source without adding significant original commentary, substantive modifications, or educational or entertainment value. ... Content that exclusively features readings of other materials you did not originally create, like text from websites or news feeds ... This policy applies even if you have permission from the original creator.
findings.applies: Tech explainers are often tempted to fill time with company keynote clips, manufacturer B-roll, press-kit renders, product promo videos, or a voice reading a research paper, article or press release. Permission or a press kit doesn't help, because this policy isn't about copyright. It applies to the channel as a whole, so a few such videos can cost monetization on all of them.
findings.action: Make your own visuals: diagrams, animations and your own screen recordings. If you show a company clip, keep it short and explain over it in your own words. Never make a video that mainly reads someone else's article, paper or announcement.

findings.topic: Branded content (free products, AI-tool sponsors)
findings.official_quote: Branded content is any content on YouTube influenced by a brand partner in exchange for something of value, such as featuring or promoting a brand’s products or services in exchange for payment, free products, or sponsorships (whether you receive the benefit now or later on). ... If your video contains branded content, you must let us know using the paid promotion declaration in Studio. ... • Hacking software
findings.applies: AI and tech channels attract AI-tool sponsors, free subscriptions, loaned phones and review units. A free AI-tool plan given in exchange for featuring it counts, even if the benefit comes later. 'Hacking software' is on the list of products branded content can never promote, which matters for security-tool sponsors. The page also says undisclosed branded content may be removed and may affect YouTube Partner Program eligibility.
findings.action: Whenever a video features a product you were paid for, given or promised anything for, tick 'paid promotion' in Studio and say so aloud in the video. Turn down sponsors that sell hacking tools.

findings.topic: Trademarks of real products
findings.official_quote: Trademark infringement is improper or unauthorized use of a trademark in a way that is likely to cause confusion as to the source of that product. YouTube policies prohibit videos and channels that infringe trademarks. If your content uses someone else’s trademarks in a way that might cause confusion, your videos can be blocked. Your channel may also be suspended.
findings.applies: Videos on phones, chips, chatbots and the cloud will name and show real brands. Naming a product to explain it isn't the problem. The risk is presentation that suggests the channel is official or affiliated: a company logo in the channel icon or banner, or thumbnails styled like a brand's own. The channel name is about to change, so this is the moment to keep brand marks out of it.
findings.action: Use brand names only to refer to the product being explained. Keep company logos and brand names out of the new channel name, icon and banner, and don't style thumbnails to look like official brand material.

review.notes:
No wording in the kit (description, ten titles, first script) conflicts with a YouTube rule I read, so there are no kit_edits.

Not YouTube rules, but worth passing to the fact-check step:
1) Script, title card: "So: no thinking ahead in sentences, no looking things up unless it's given a tool to do so." states an argued-over point as settled. Interpretability research, for example Anthropic's 2025 work on rhyming, reported that models can plan words ahead internally. The channel description promises "Where something is uncertain or still argued over, the video says so." Suggested replacement: "So: it writes one piece at a time. Researchers have found signs that it plans a few words ahead inside, but it still outputs one piece at a time, and it doesn't look things up unless it's given a tool to do so." I didn't verify this research here.
2) Title "What 'The Cloud' Really Is (It's a Building)": the cloud is many data centres. Make sure the video says so, or use "(It's Buildings Full of Computers)". I didn't read YouTube's misleading-metadata policy, so this is not a rule finding.

Other official points:
- The YPP policy "AI Personas Related to Sensitive Topics" (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/1311392) doesn't apply now. It would if the channel added an AI-generated presenter giving health, legal, financial or political advice. Quote: "This includes any content that presents itself as a human expert providing advice to viewers on topics such as health, legal issues, finances, or politics." Keep any future AI host away from topics like 'AI stocks'.
- Made for kids: the official page lists "Animated content that appeals to everyone" as general audience. But "Whether the language of the video is intended for children to understand" and "characters ... that appeal to children, including animated characters or cartoon figures" are factors toward made for kids. Keep the plain-language, simple-picture style aimed at adults, and avoid child-style mascots and 'for kids' wording in metadata.
- Many blogs claim AI voiceovers are banned from monetization. No official page I read says that. The monetization page says: "If you use automated tools or templates to help create your content, the final product must still demonstrate your creative vision and provide educational or entertainment value."
- The branded content page also says: "If our systems detect your video includes branded content you have not disclosed, we may automatically apply a branded content label to your video and notify you."

Every page below was read with the reader, and none returned COULD NOT READ. I did not read, edit or commit anything in the repository, and wrote no files.

findings.topic: AI-generated realistic space imagery must be disclosed
findings.official_quote: Creators must disclose GenAI content that: • Makes a real person appear to say or do something they didn’t do. • Alters footage of a real event or place. • Generates a realistic scene that didn’t actually occur. • Creates music that’s the main focus of the video. ... Examples of content, edits, or video assistance that creators don’t need to disclose: ... Using an AI-generated or altered animation of a missile in a fully animated video ... Production assistance, like using generative AI tools to create or improve a video outline, script, thumbnail, title, or infographic ... Note: Disclosing AI content alone won’t limit a video’s audience or impact its eligibility to earn money. ... Creators who consistently choose not to disclose this information may be subject to manual application of a label, or penalties from YouTube, including removal of content or suspension from the YouTube Partner Program.
findings.applies: Space channels lean on photoreal renders of things nobody has filmed. On this list, a photoreal AI sequence of Earth going dark (title 3), the inside of a black hole (7), the biggest star (4), Voyager drifting in deep space (9) or the surface of Mars (10) is a realistic scene that didn't happen or AI footage of a real place, so it needs the 'AI use: Yes' answer. Using AI to extend, fill in or add detail to a real NASA or ESA image counts as 'Alters footage of a real event or place'. Upscaling or sharpening doesn't. The first script's flat graphics (torch, a line racing to the Moon, a counter) are plainly animation and need no disclosure, and neither do AI-written outlines, scripts, titles or thumbnails. Disclosing doesn't cut reach or earnings. Failing to disclose again and again can get videos removed or the channel suspended from the Partner Program.
findings.action: On every upload, answer the 'AI use' question in Attributes: Yes when any photoreal AI image or clip of a real object, place or event appears, or when AI changed a real space image beyond sharpening or upscaling. No when the AI art is clearly cartoon or diagram-style. When unsure, choose Yes. Never use an AI copy of a real scientist's or astronaut's voice or face.

findings.topic: Reused content (NASA/ESA footage on its own does not count as yours)
findings.official_quote: Reused content refers to channels that repurpose content that’s already on YouTube or another online source without adding significant original commentary, substantive modifications, or educational or entertainment value. ... Our reused content policy applies to your channel as a whole. If you have videos that violate our guidelines, or if we cannot clearly tell that you made the content, monetization may be removed from your entire channel. ... This policy applies even if you have permission from the original creator. Reused content is separate from YouTube’s Copyright enforcement, which means it’s not based on copyright, permission, or fair use. ... • Content uploaded many times by other creators ... • Reused content from other online sources where the creator is either visible in the content or explains how the creator added to the content
findings.applies: This is the biggest monetization risk for a faceless space channel. NASA launch replays, ISS Earth views and JWST images appear on thousands of channels, and YouTube says outright that being public domain or having permission doesn't help. Reviewers also read the channel description. The current description doesn't break the rule, but 'clear pictures' doesn't tell a reviewer the pictures are the channel's own work. The first script (original animations carrying a narrated argument) is the safe pattern.
findings.action: Build every video on its own script, narration and animation, like the light-year script. Use agency photos and clips only as short supporting shots that the narration explains. Never upload raw agency footage, launch replays, 'Earth from the ISS' loops or image slideshows. Change the description so it says what the channel makes itself.

kit_edit.quote: Each video answers a single question with real numbers and clear pictures, and links the sources underneath.
kit_edit.replace_with: Each video answers a single question with real numbers and pictures made for the channel, and links the sources underneath. Telescope and spacecraft images are credited on screen, and artist's impressions are labelled as artist's impressions.

findings.topic: Generic or repetitive (template-made) content
findings.official_quote: Generic or repetitive content includes content that looks like it’s made with a template, or that may feel repetitive to viewers after watching several videos in a row from the same channel. ... What’s important is that the substance of each video should be materially varied and deliver creative, educational, or other value. ... • Same intro and outro for your videos, but the bulk of your content is different ... • Image slideshows, templated storylines, or scrolling text with minimal or no narrative, commentary, or educational value • AI-generated content made with generic or unoriginal templates giving the impression of mass production without adding the creator’s original, authentic insights or perspective
findings.applies: The 'one question at a time' series format is fine: YouTube allows a shared intro and outro when the bulk of each video differs. A faceless format becomes a problem if videos turn into interchangeable stock-footage-plus-voice slideshows, or into AI-generated scripts and visuals pushed out on a template with nothing added. Reviewers look at the main theme, most-viewed videos, newest videos and metadata, so a few weak, rushed uploads can sink the whole channel's application.
findings.action: Give every video its own argument and its own visuals, as the first script does (the torch, the Moon line, the Voyager comparison). Keep the shared part to the intro, outro and title card. Don't batch-produce videos from one template or from unedited AI output.

findings.topic: Agency imagery: only U.S. government work is automatically public domain
findings.official_quote: Public domain refers to content not protected by copyright because the copyright has expired or the content wasn’t eligible for copyright protection. For example, works created by U.S. government agencies are automatically in the public domain. ... Ultimately, it's your responsibility to verify that a work is in the public domain before you upload it to YouTube.
findings.applies: Work made by NASA as a U.S. government agency falls under this rule. Much of what people call 'NASA imagery' doesn't: ESA, CSA and observatory images, images co-credited to universities or institutes, and third-party photos hosted on agency sites. YouTube's monetization page (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2490020) adds: "You can monetize royalty-free or Creative Commons content when the license agreement grants you rights to use it commercially." and "Although you may have found the content online free of charge, usually its actual creator holds many of the rights needed to commercially exploit the content." It also says: "If you prove that the content in your video is part of the public domain, you can monetize." So every non-NASA image needs a licence that allows commercial use, and the channel needs to be able to show where each image came from.
findings.action: Keep a source log for every video: file, page URL, credit line exactly as published, and licence. Use an image only when its credit line shows it is U.S.-government-made or its licence allows commercial use. Credit each image on screen or in the description, in the form YouTube suggests for Creative Commons: title, author, source URL, licence.

findings.topic: Content ID claims on public-domain NASA footage
findings.official_quote: You must have exclusive rights to the material in the reference file for the territories where you claim ownership. The following examples are ineligible for use in or as a reference: • Content licensed non-exclusively from a third party • Content released under Creative Commons or similar free of charge/open licenses • Public domain footage, recordings, or compositions
findings.applies: Space channels often get automated claims from footage libraries that uploaded NASA clips as their own. YouTube's dispute page (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2797454) says these "are NOT legitimate reasons to dispute a claim: • Giving credit to the copyright owner" and warns: "Repeated or malicious abuse of the dispute process can result in penalties against your video or channel." The claim-status page (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/106990) lists a dispute type: "Public Domain: Disputes filed because the uploader claims the content claimed in their video is in the public domain and is no longer protected by copyright." A credit in the description is not a defence. The source log is.
findings.action: If a claim lands on a clip whose source log shows it was made by NASA, dispute it as public domain and cite the NASA source page. If the clip is ESA, third-party or unlogged, don't dispute: remove or replace the clip.

findings.topic: Misleading realistic visuals and hypothetical scenarios
findings.official_quote: Unsatisfying or off-putting content refers to content that relies heavily on emotionally manipulative formulas, mimics existing formats or stories to a degree that the videos feel interchangeable, or appears designed to shock or surprise viewers for the sole purpose of getting views. ... • Content that utilizes creative tools to assist in delivering a unique, well-researched, or creative narrative, like using AI to edit your video scripts or generate a unique background visual for your content ... • Content that uses deceptive or misleading imagery or narratives, such as realistic visuals tricking viewers into believing a fake celebrity death or natural disaster has occurred
findings.applies: Title 3 ('What Would Happen If the Sun Vanished for a Day?') and title 7 (black hole interiors) invite realistic disaster or 'first image' visuals. The titles themselves are honest: 'What would happen if' and 'What We Know and Don't'. The risk is thumbnails or footage that look like a real event or a real telescope photo. Space channels are known for 'NASA just captured...' thumbnails built on renders.
findings.action: Keep hypotheticals framed as hypotheticals in the title, thumbnail and on screen (for example a small 'Hypothetical' or 'Illustration' tag). Label every artist's impression or simulation as one. Never present a render as a photograph.

findings.topic: Misinformation policy (low exposure, but watch archive footage and links)
findings.official_quote: Manipulated content: Content that has been technically manipulated or doctored in a way that misleads users (usually beyond clips taken out of context) and may pose a serious risk of egregious harm. • Misattributed content: Content that may pose a serious risk of egregious harm by falsely claiming that old footage from a past event is from a current event. ... Please note these policies also apply to external links in your content. ... We may allow content that violates the misinformation policies noted on this page if that content includes additional context in the video, audio, title, or description.
findings.applies: The policy as currently published covers census suppression, manipulated content and misattributed content, all tied to 'serious risk of egregious harm'. It doesn't police ordinary science mistakes, so careful explainers like these are at low risk. The real exposure for a space channel is news-style videos: passing off old solar-flare, fireball, launch-failure or asteroid footage as a current event. The source links under each video are covered by the policy too.
findings.action: Date any archive footage on screen when it could be taken for current news ('2017 flare', 'Archive: 1990'). Link only to primary or reputable sources (agency pages, journals, observatories), never to sites pushing hoaxes, even to debunk them.

findings.topic: Agency logos and branding (impersonation and trademarks)
findings.official_quote: Impersonation may include deceptively copying the branding, content, or usernames of individuals, channels or entities. ... YouTube also enforces trademark holder rights. ... It should be obvious to your viewers that your channel doesn't represent the original creator, artist, or entity.
findings.applies: Many faceless space channels use the NASA 'meatball', ESA logos or mission patches in their avatar, banner, watermark or thumbnails, which can look like an official agency channel and invites trademark complaints. The kit has no branding yet, so this is a rule for the coming redesign and thumbnails.
findings.action: Keep agency logos, seals and mission insignia out of the avatar, banner, watermark and thumbnails, and don't use 'Official' or agency names in the channel name or handle. If needed, add one line to the About section saying the channel is independent and not affiliated with NASA or ESA.

findings.topic: NASA and ESA's own media terms (logos, third-party images, ESA commercial use)
findings.applies: This is not a YouTube rule. These are the agencies' own terms, but nasa.gov and esa.int couldn't be opened in this session (the network blocked both), so the wording here comes only from search-result excerpts of those pages. Check it on the pages before relying on it. According to those excerpts: NASA's general permission does not cover the NASA insignia ('meatball'), logotype ('worm') or seal, which need explicit permission. NASA marks third-party copyrighted material on its sites, and users must contact that copyright holder directly. NASA content must not imply NASA endorses a product. ESA's standard terms bar commercial use without written authorisation, while ESA items labelled CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO may be reused with credit and under the licence conditions. A monetized channel is a commercial use, so plain ESA-copyright items can't be used without permission.
findings.action: Before using any ESA image or video, check its copyright line: use it only if it says CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO (credit ESA and follow the licence), otherwise skip it or ask ESA in writing. For NASA, use only items with a plain NASA credit, and treat anything marked with another copyright holder as third-party. Read both agency pages once from a connection that can reach them.

review.audience_setting: Not made for kids. YouTube says \"General audience content is content that could appeal to everyone, but isn’t intended specifically for children, or content that is intended for a teen or older audience. General audience content should be set as “not made for kids.”\" and that a video isn't made for kids just because \"It’s safe or appropriate for everyone to watch\". These explainers use adult-level language (trillions of kilometres, light-years) with no child characters, songs or kid-targeted metadata, so this applies. Re-check any single video that adds a cartoon mascot, simple kids' language or kid-targeted titles.
review.notes:
COULD NOT READ: nasa.gov (www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/) and esa.int (www.esa.int/ESA_Multimedia/Copyright_Notice_Images) are not allowed by this session's network settings, so the one unofficial finding about the agencies' own terms rests on search-result excerpts only. Both hosts would have to be allowed in the session's network settings to read the pages directly.

Changes since the blogs: the monetization policies page (read today) has replaced the old 'inauthentic content' heading with four sections: 'Generic or Repetitive Content', 'Reused content', 'Unsatisfying or Off-putting Content' and 'AI Personas Related to Sensitive Topics' (space is not one of the sensitive topics listed). The misinformation page now lists only census suppression, manipulated content and misattributed content, so blog claims that YouTube removes 'science misinformation' in general are not supported by the current page.

AI narration: the GenAI disclosure page does not list a generic synthetic narrator voice as something that must be disclosed. It explicitly exempts 'Cloning one’s own voice to create voice overs or dubs' and says disclosed non-music AI audio gets a description label. It requires disclosure for AI music 'that’s the main focus of the video', so take background music from YouTube's Audio Library to avoid the question.

Script check (not a rule issue): the numbers hold up. Light circles Earth about 7.5 times a second, the Moon is about 1.3 light-seconds away, the Sun about 8 min 20 s, a light-year is about 9.46 trillion km, Proxima is about 4.24 light-years away, and at about 17 km/s Voyager would take about 75,000 years to cover that distance. One line is off: under '[Night sky]', 'You see that star as it was more than four years ago' implies Proxima Centauri can be seen in the night sky, but it is far too faint to see without a telescope. Suggested fix: 'If you could see it, you'd be seeing it as it was more than four years ago.' Or switch the line to Alpha Centauri, about 4.4 light-years away and visible to the naked eye from the Southern Hemisphere.

review.audience_setting: Not made for kids. YouTube says "General audience content is content that could appeal to everyone, but isn’t intended specifically for children, or content that is intended for a teen or older audience. General audience content should be set as “not made for kids.”" It lists "Animated content that appeals to everyone" as an example, and it notes that content with violence "is likely not made for kids" (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9528076).

findings.topic: Denying or minimising well-documented atrocities ("both sides")
findings.official_quote: Denial or minimization of a well-documented, major violent event or the victimhood of such an event.
findings.applies: YouTube's hate speech policy lists this line, and the same page lists "Victims of a major violent event and their kin" as a protected group. Several of the first ten titles run straight into such events: the Ottoman video (1915), Africa's borders (the Congo Free State, the Herero and Nama killings), Poland (the Holocaust), Britain (colonial famines and massacres) and Russia (Soviet-era famines). The channel description promises "Where historians disagree, both sides are shown." Applied to an atrocity that is well documented but politically denied, that promise invites a script to present the denial as "the other side", which this policy treats as hate speech. YouTube does not publish a list of which events count, so the examples above are my judgment, not YouTube's list.
findings.action: Change the description line as shown. In scripts, state well-documented atrocities as fact and name the sources. Where a government denies one, say so as a political position and say in the narration itself what historians conclude, because YouTube requires that context to be "in the images or audio of the video itself".

kit_edit.quote: Where historians disagree, both sides are shown.
kit_edit.replace_with: Where historians disagree, the main views and their evidence are shown.

findings.topic: Graphic archive images: context in the video, or removal or 18+
findings.official_quote: For educational content containing the kinds of violent or graphic content noted above, this context must appear in the images or audio of the video itself. Providing it in the title or description is insufficient. … Age-restricted content isn’t viewable to anyone who’s under 18 years of age or signed out.
findings.applies: Animated maps carry no graphic content, and the Roman script is clean. The risk arrives when later videos reach for archive material: atrocity photographs from the Congo Free State, famine photographs, Second World War and Holocaust footage, or massacre art for the Mongol and Khwarazm videos. The kit's "Dates and sources are listed under every video" will not protect such images, because the context has to be in the picture or the narration. Even with context, YouTube may age-restrict instead of removing the video. That hides it from under-18s and signed-out viewers, a big share of a history audience, and the age-restriction page adds that such videos "may have limited or no ads monetization". The same policy weighs "Whether violent imagery or audio has been blurred, masked, or obscured" and "The amount of time the violent images or audio is in the content."
findings.action: Tell the story with maps, dated text cards and non-graphic period art. If a graphic archive image is essential, show it briefly, blur it, keep it out of the thumbnail and the opening seconds, and have the narration say what it shows, where, when and why it is shown while it is on screen. After uploading, check YouTube Studio for a "Viewable by 18+" notice.

findings.topic: Ads on war content: non-graphic is fine, gore is limited
findings.official_quote: Non-graphic educational coverage or discussion of war and/or conflict. … Dead bodies with obvious injury or damage in educational or documentary settings (such as a history learning channel); graphic game violence in thumbnail; raw footage of armed conflict without injuries; description of graphic details of tragedies; dramatized content displaying severe and shocking injuries.
findings.applies: The first sentence sits in the Violence section's "can earn ad revenue" block and describes this channel's map format exactly. The second sentence opens the next block, which by the page's order (can earn / limited / no ad earnings) is limited ads. The reader did not print the tier heading for that block, so confirm it on the page. It names "a history learning channel" by name. The same block lists "Highly graphic descriptions of tragedies (in the form of audio or video)", so narration that lingers on how people died also limits ads, for example the Mongol sacks of Nishapur and Urgench or the falls of Constantinople in 1204 and 1453. The page says the rules cover the "thumbnail, title, description, and tags".
findings.action: Give the scale of killings as numbers with sources, not graphic detail. Keep thumbnails to maps, arrows, dates and non-graphic period art: no wounds, corpses or skull piles. Never drop in unnarrated raw battle footage. Answer the monetisation self-certification questionnaire honestly for each video.

findings.topic: Reused content: archive and public-domain material
findings.official_quote: Reused content refers to channels that repurpose content that’s already on YouTube or another online source without adding significant original commentary, substantive modifications, or educational or entertainment value. … This policy applies even if you have permission from the original creator. Reused content is separate from YouTube’s Copyright enforcement, which means it’s not based on copyright, permission, or fair use. … Content that exclusively features readings of other materials you did not originally create, like text from websites or news feeds
findings.applies: History channels lean on public-domain newsreels, Wikimedia maps and paintings, and clips from other documentaries. Public domain or permission does not exempt any of it from this monetisation rule. The page also lists "Content uploaded many times by other creators", which describes famous newsreels. It says the policy "applies to your channel as a whole" and that "if we cannot clearly tell that you made the content, monetization may be removed from your entire channel." Reviewers check videos, the channel description, titles and video descriptions. A script that paraphrases or reads out Wikipedia would also fall under the last quoted line.
findings.action: Make original map animation and original narration the substance of every video, and use archive material only as short supporting shots under the narration, never in long unnarrated stretches. Write each script in your own words from several sources. If it is true, add a line to the channel description saying every map is drawn and every script is written for this channel, so a reviewer can see who made the content.

findings.topic: Inauthentic (templated) content
findings.official_quote: Generic or repetitive content includes content that looks like it’s made with a template, or that may feel repetitive to viewers after watching several videos in a row from the same channel. … Image slideshows, templated storylines, or scrolling text with minimal or no narrative, commentary, or educational value
findings.applies: The format is deliberately a template: "Each documentary follows one line on the map and explains why it moved." That is allowed when every video delivers its own research and story. The risk is a run of near-identical "how X got so big" videos built on the same base map, pacing, music and voice, made quickly. The page says reviewers focus on the channel's "Main theme" and its "Video metadata (including titles, thumbnails, and descriptions)", and it lists "Content that repeatedly uses disturbing themes (such as violence or loss) without building a cohesive narrative" as unsatisfying content, a real risk for a war-heavy history channel.
findings.action: Give each video its own argument, sources and visual ideas beyond the base map, as the Roman script does with its "too big to run" thesis. Don't batch-produce videos from one script skeleton. Keep the titles as varied as the current ten.

findings.topic: Public domain and credit for archive maps, art and footage
findings.official_quote: Ultimately, it's your responsibility to verify that a work is in the public domain before you upload it to YouTube. With this said, verifying public domain status can be complicated, since there's no official list of works in the public domain.
findings.applies: Old maps, paintings and newsreels are the channel's raw material, but copyright terms differ by country, and footage libraries often hold Content ID claims on newsreels. YouTube's copyright myths page (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2797449) says "Giving credit to the copyright owner doesn’t automatically give you the rights to use their copyrighted content", although CC BY works may be used with attribution. The dispute page lists giving credit and not monetising as "NOT legitimate reasons to dispute a claim". The kit's habit of listing sources under every video is good for credits but does not establish rights.
findings.action: Keep a per-video asset log (item, source, licence, date of creation or death of the author). Draw base maps from public-domain data. Use only items whose public-domain status or licence you have checked, and credit CC BY items in the description. Dispute a Content ID claim only when you are sure of your rights.

findings.topic: AI 'talking' historical figures describing their deaths
findings.official_quote: Content that realistically simulates deceased or abused individuals describing their death or violence experienced.
findings.applies: This is listed as a harassment violation, which means removal and possible strikes. Faceless history channels often animate portraits with AI voices. A realistic AI Constantine XI narrating the fall of Constantinople in 1453, or a massacre victim telling their story in the first person, would match this line. The policy sets no time limit on "deceased", so applying it to people dead for centuries is my reading of the plain wording.
findings.action: Don't make realistic AI-animated historical people speak about their own deaths or the violence done to them. Have the narrator quote real primary sources and name the source.

findings.topic: Russia video and the war in Ukraine (sensitive events)
findings.official_quote: March 23, 2022: Due to the war in Ukraine, content that exploits, dismisses, or condones the war is ineligible for monetization until further notice. … Using keywords related to a sensitive event to attempt to drive additional traffic.
findings.applies: "How Russia Got So Big" will naturally run up to the present map. If it ends by showing Crimea or other occupied regions as ordinary Russian territory, or presents 2014 and 2022 as one more step in natural growth, it risks being read as condoning the war and losing ads. That reading is mine; YouTube gives no map-specific guidance. The second line (an example of what may not be monetised) means Ukraine-war keywords used for traffic can lose ads even on a history video.
findings.action: Either end the Russia story at 1991 and say so, or show areas occupied since 2014 and 2022 as occupied, in the narration and on the map. Keep "Ukraine war" terms out of that video's title and tags unless the video is genuinely about it.

findings.topic: Disputed borders: no YouTube rule, but country blocks under local law
findings.official_quote: YouTube may block specific content to comply with local laws
findings.applies: I searched YouTube Help and blog.youtube and found no YouTube rule on how to draw borders or disputed territories; any blog that claims one is not quoting YouTube. The only official risk is a block in a particular country after a legal complaint (the Legal policies page, https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/3001497, says the team "answers requests to block videos on legal grounds"). Which countries have laws about maps or about events such as 1915 or Kashmir is outside YouTube's pages and was not checked here.
findings.action: Pick one border convention and use it in every video: borders as actually controlled at the date shown, with disputed areas hatched and labelled as disputed. Expect that a video may occasionally be blocked in one country. That is a local block, not a strike.

findings.topic: Made for kids
findings.official_quote: General audience content is content that could appeal to everyone, but isn’t intended specifically for children, or content that is intended for a teen or older audience. General audience content should be set as “not made for kids.” … Animated content that appeals to everyone
findings.applies: Bright animated maps could look child-friendly, but the subject is wars and empires for a general audience, and the page says content with violence "is likely not made for kids." Setting it wrongly has consequences "on YouTube" and under COPPA. The age-restriction page notes that "made for kids" settings "won't impact age restrictions".
findings.action: In YouTube Studio > Settings > Channel > Advanced settings, choose "No, set this channel as not made for kids". Avoid cartoon mascots and kid-targeted wording ("for kids", school grade levels) in titles and tags.

findings.topic: AI disclosure on upload
findings.official_quote: We require creators to disclose AI-generated or altered content that seems realistic. … Using an AI-generated or altered animation of a missile in a fully animated video … Disclosing AI content alone won’t limit a video’s audience or impact its eligibility to earn money.
findings.applies: Animated maps are not realistic, so videos like the Roman script need no disclosure. The page requires it for content that "Alters footage of a real event or place" or "Generates a realistic scene that didn’t actually occur", which would cover AI-made photo-real battle scenes, colourised or altered archive footage beyond simple repair, or realistic reconstructions of historic cities. It also lists "AI generated music" among things to disclose. Using AI to help write the script, or cloning your own voice for narration, needs no disclosure.
findings.action: On every upload, answer "AI use" No for map-only videos. Answer Yes whenever a video contains realistic AI imagery of real places, events or people, or AI-generated music. Disclosing costs nothing.

review.notes:
The kit's ten titles and the Roman script break no YouTube rule: no graphic wording, no shock words, and the script is purely political and geographic. The real exposure comes later, from archive images, atrocity topics (Ottoman, Africa, Poland, Britain, Russia) and the Russia video's ending map. The only kit text that should change is the "both sides" promise in the description.

Two points for the fact-check, not YouTube rules: "How Mongolia Conquered Half the World in One Lifetime" names the modern country rather than the Mongol Empire, and the empire peaked after Genghis Khan's death. And Egypt's borders are mostly straight lines; it is the inhabited land that follows the Nile, so that video must explain the title.

Caveat on the advertiser-friendly page: the reader printed the tier headings only for the profanity section. The Violence section's tiers are inferred from the page's fixed order (can earn / limited / no ad earnings), so confirm the yellow/limited label on the live page.

The policy-updates page (support.google.com/youtube/answer/10008196) lists no 2025–2026 change to the educational/documentary violence rules. The Nov 2025 and Apr 2025 violence changes concern video games and scripted live-action content, not this format.

Housekeeping: I briefly saved one page's text to /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Jachi/8146f71f-73d7-5544-b4d0-28b8048fbb36/scratchpad/yt/factcheck/afg5.txt and deleted it right away; no other files were written. I did not touch the website repository.

review.audience_setting: Not made for kids: these are slow history stories written for adults falling asleep, and YouTube says "General audience content should be set as “not made for kids.”" It also says a video is not made for kids just because "It’s safe or appropriate for everyone to watch" or "Children may incidentally see it". Set this once at channel level and keep children's story cues out of the titles and thumbnails, because YouTube "may override your audience setting choice in cases of error or abuse."

findings.topic: Long videos need a verified account
findings.official_quote: By default, you can upload videos that are up to 15 minutes long. Verified accounts can upload videos longer than 15 minutes.
findings.applies: Every video in this format runs far past 15 minutes. The first title says "(2 Hours)". Until the account is verified, the channel cannot publish its format at all. The same page sets the upper limit: "The maximum file size you can upload is 256 GB or 12 hours, whichever is less." It also warns: "After you verify your account, you’ll need to upload your video again". On the feature table at https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9890437, "Longer videos (>15 mins)" is an Intermediate feature that needs phone verification, and "Apply for monetization" is an Advanced feature.
findings.action: Verify the channel's phone number in YouTube Studio (Settings > Channel > Feature eligibility) before the first upload, then confirm that "Features that require a phone verification" shows Enabled. Keep every video under 12 hours.

findings.topic: Phone verification limit
findings.official_quote: To help prevent abuse, a phone number can only be associated with 2 channels per year.
findings.applies: This channel cannot post a single full-length video without phone verification. The owner is setting up several channels, so one number covers only two of them per year. If this channel is third in line for a used number, it cannot upload long videos.
findings.action: Before launch, decide which phone number verifies this channel, and keep a list of which numbers verified which channels and when. Verify the long-form channels first, because they cannot post at all without it.

findings.topic: AI mass-production (spam policy, can end the channel)
findings.official_quote: Automated or synthetic mass-production: Using automated tools or AI to churn out high volumes of similar content with minimal changes. While testing out new creation tools or posting a few variations of a video is ok, we don't allow use of these tools to flood our platform with repetitive content. This includes coordinated mass-production and technical manipulation to bypass filters or trick viewers. Example: Channels that use the exact same background music and repetitive AI generated imagery across many videos, with each video reading out an AI-generated script.
findings.applies: This is a Community Guidelines rule, not only a monetization rule: "If your content violates this policy, we may suspend your monetization or terminate your channel or account." YouTube's own example closely matches the usual way faceless sleep-history channels are made: one constant music bed (the kit promises "no music changes"), slow AI images, and an AI voice reading an AI-written script, published at volume. Long, low-variation videos make this channel unusually exposed.
findings.action: Do not let any video be a same-music, same-look, AI-read AI script. Vary the sound bed by setting (monastery, harbour, farm), give each video its own visuals, and have a person research and write or substantially rewrite each script. Publish at a pace where each video is genuinely made, not in bulk.

findings.topic: Generic or repetitive content (monetization review)
findings.official_quote: What’s important is that the substance of each video should be materially varied and deliver creative, educational, or other value.
findings.applies: Videos that YouTube lists as not allowed to monetize include "AI-generated content made with generic or unoriginal templates giving the impression of mass production without adding the creator’s original, authentic insights or perspective". The same page allows "Content that utilizes creative tools to assist in delivering a unique, well-researched, or creative narrative, like using AI to edit your video scripts or generate a unique background visual for your content". Reviewers look at the "Channel’s “About” section" and "Video metadata". The kit's titles cover distinct topics, which helps. The channel description, however, says nothing about the research or writing, which is this format's main evidence of value.
findings.action: Make each video's substance clearly different: new facts, a new place, a new period. List the main sources in every video description. Add a line to the About text saying the stories are researched and written for the channel, but only once that is true.

kit_edit.quote: Put one on, turn the screen down, and let it go on without you.
kit_edit.replace_with:
Put one on, turn the screen down, and let it go on without you.

Every story is researched and written for this channel, and the main sources are listed under each video.

findings.topic: Made for kids (bedtime stories)
findings.official_quote: Whether the video includes songs, stories, or poems for children.
findings.applies: This bedtime-story factor is the one that could pull a sleep channel toward "made for kids". The kit's stories are adult history, in adult language, with no characters or cues aimed at children, so they are general-audience content. The same page also counts "Whether children are your intended audience (e.g. as indicated in your video metadata)". The current description doesn't conflict with this, but it doesn't state the intended audience either, and https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9527654 says YouTube "may override your audience setting choice in cases of error or abuse."
findings.action: In YouTube Studio > Settings > Channel > Advanced settings, choose "No, set this channel as not made for kids." Keep "bedtime story", "for kids" and cartoon-style thumbnails out of titles, tags and art, and state the adult audience in the description.

kit_edit.quote: Quiet history for falling asleep.
kit_edit.replace_with: Quiet history to fall asleep to, written for adults.

findings.topic: Mid-roll ads on sleep content
findings.official_quote: While YouTube can automatically suggest the best placement for mid-roll ads, you may want to turn off mid-roll ads if not appropriate. For example, meditation videos may not be suitable for mid-roll ads.
findings.applies: The description promises "no adverts in the middle of the story where we can avoid them". Once the channel is monetized, every 2-hour video is eligible for mid-rolls ("On monetized videos that are 8 minutes or longer"). The same page also says: "By default, automatic mid-roll ad slots are selected for your video." If the defaults are left on, ads will be placed inside the story, breaking the description's promise.
findings.action: When monetized, go to Studio > Settings > Upload defaults > Monetization and leave "Show mid-roll ads during my videos" unchecked. Alternatively, use only manual slots at a chapter break near the start and uncheck "Automatic ad slots". Turning mid-rolls off lowers ad revenue; that trade-off is the owner's call.

findings.topic: Ads can appear before monetization
findings.official_quote: Ads may appear on your uploaded videos even if you haven’t monetized the videos yourself.
findings.applies: The same page adds: "YouTube may also place ads on videos in channels not in the YouTube Partner Program." Rights holders can also place ads on a video that uses their music. Before the channel joins YPP, it cannot fully control ads in its stories. The kit's hedge ("where we can avoid them") is accurate as written.
findings.action: Keep the hedge "where we can avoid them" and never change it to "no ads" or "ad-free". Use only music you own or have licensed with no Content ID claims, so no rights holder adds ads.

findings.topic: AI disclosure (images, music, voice)
findings.official_quote: Creators must disclose GenAI content that: Makes a real person appear to say or do something they didn’t do. Alters footage of a real event or place. Generates a realistic scene that didn’t actually occur. Creates music that’s the main focus of the video.
findings.applies: The script calls for visuals such as "a stone corridor, one candle". If these are photorealistic AI images of real places (Hadrian's Wall, a Roman bakery, a Viking harbour), they fall under "Generates a realistic scene that didn’t actually occur". The page also lists "AI generated extra footage of a real place" and "AI generated music" as needing disclosure. Using AI to write the script does not need disclosure ("Production assistance, like using generative AI tools to create or improve a video outline, script, thumbnail, title, or infographic"), and neither does "Cloning one’s own voice to create voice overs or dubs". The page does not list a stock AI narration voice as needing disclosure on its own. Disclosure costs nothing: "Disclosing AI content alone won’t limit a video’s audience or impact its eligibility to earn money."
findings.action: On every upload, answer the "AI use" question: Yes if the video has photorealistic AI scenes or AI-generated music, No for painterly or illustrated art with a human-made or licensed music bed. For the narration, use a stock voice or the owner's own cloned voice, never a clone of a real narrator or celebrity (impersonation policy, support.google.com/youtube/answer/2801947).

findings.topic: AI narrator giving sleep or health advice
findings.official_quote: This includes any content that presents itself as a human expert providing advice to viewers on topics such as health, legal issues, finances, or politics.
findings.applies: This sleep channel is unusually exposed: an AI-voiced narrator could easily slip into insomnia tips or claims that the videos improve sleep. YouTube's example of what can't be monetized is "An AI “doctor” providing medical diagnoses, health advice, or wellness remedies". The current kit is fine: the narrator only says "If you drift off partway through, that is exactly what this is for."
findings.action: Keep the narrator to history. No sleep tips, insomnia or anxiety advice, breathing exercises presented as therapy, or claims of health benefits, whether in scripts, titles or descriptions.

findings.topic: Reused content: reading texts you didn't write
findings.official_quote: Content that exclusively features readings of other materials you did not originally create, like text from websites or news feeds
findings.applies: Long history narration tempts creators to read out encyclopedia articles or public-domain books, such as the Rule of Benedict quoted in the first script. That would make the channel ineligible to monetize even with no copyright claim, because the page says reused content "is separate from YouTube’s Copyright enforcement". The kit's opening script is original writing that paraphrases the Rule, which is fine.
findings.action: Write every script in your own words. Quote sources only briefly, and never narrate a whole article, chapter or translation as the video.

findings.topic: Title promises (durations)
findings.official_quote: Malicious clickbait: Using maliciously misleading titles, thumbnails, descriptions, or imagery to trick users into clicking on a video that does not deliver what was promised.
findings.applies: "A Quiet Night in a Medieval Monastery (2 Hours)" promises two hours. Sleep channels often fill such a runtime with a looped story or ambience. YouTube's example is a title that "offers a full sports match but the video shows only a clip".
findings.action: Use a duration in a title only when the story itself fills that time. If part of the runtime is ambience after the story ends, say so in the description and chapters, and never loop the narration to reach a length.

review.notes: Every page read printed normally (no COULD NOT READ). The channel name was ignored as instructed. On AI narration: no official page says an AI voice is banned.
