The risk is the template, spelled out in the spam policy's mass-production example and the monetization page's \"Generic or Repetitive Content\" section. Unofficial only: third-party sites (Tubefilter, TechRepublic, The Next Web, July 2026) report that YouTube reworked its inauthentic-content guidance into three categories. The live official page matches that structure (Generic or Repetitive, Unsatisfying or Off-putting, AI Personas Related to Sensitive Topics), so the findings quote the page directly. Claims that enforcement targets faceless channels in general appear only in third-party commentary and are not official. YPP eligibility: https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/72851 lists \"Have advanced features access on YouTube\" and 4,000 qualified watch hours from public long-form videos. Unlisted, private and deleted videos and unconverted livestreams don't count, so test uploads left unlisted earn nothing toward the threshold. Both kit_edits are suggested improvements tied to official factors (intended audience in metadata; the About section reviewers check). Neither fixes wording that breaks a rule outright, and the research line should go in only once it is true.

review.audience_setting: Not made for kids. YouTube's Help Center says: "General audience content is content that could appeal to everyone, but isn't intended specifically for children, or content that is intended for a teen or older audience. General audience content should be set as 'not made for kids.'" Historic crime told from court records is meant for teens and adults. The illustrations don't change this, because YouTube lists "Animated content that appeals to everyone" as general audience. Set it for the whole channel and for each upload, and keep kid-targeted words and characters out of titles, tags and thumbnails.

findings.topic: Doxxing: addresses and phone numbers in court files, police reports and newspaper scans
findings.official_quote: Content that shares, threatens to share, or encourages others to share non-public personally identifiable information (PII). ... PII includes, but isn’t limited to, home addresses; email addresses; sign-in credentials, like a username or password; phone numbers; passport numbers; medical records; bank account information; or the name of a school a minor attends. (Harassment policy.) The EDSA page also lists among content that may not get an exception: "Content that reveals an individual’s private information, such as their home address, email addresses, sign-in credentials, phone numbers, passport number, or bank account information (doxxing)"
findings.applies: The whole channel is built on primary documents: court files, police reports, FBI files and newspapers. These often print home addresses, phone numbers and account details of defendants, witnesses, tipsters and victims. This matters most for recent cases with living people: Hatton Garden (2015), Antwerp (2003), the Gardner heist (1990) and the D. B. Cooper files, which name many tipsters and suspects. Doxxing is on YouTube's list of content that may not get an EDSA exception, so a 'documentary' framing does not save a video that shows an address on screen.
findings.action: Before any document or news clipping goes on screen, blur every home address, phone number, account number and ID number, and any minor's school. Do this even for people who died long ago, and even if the page is already online somewhere, unless it is clearly 'widely available public information' such as a business address.

findings.topic: Real people in mugshots and photos: privacy complaints, including from families of the dead
findings.official_quote: We also consider public interest, newsworthiness, consent, and whether the information is otherwise publicly available. ... A close family member makes the claim for a deceased individual. ... If we remove your video for a privacy violation, do not upload another version featuring the same people.
findings.applies: Mugshots, custody photos and newspaper portraits show 'uniquely identifiable' people. Some are alive, such as Hatton Garden gang members, members of the Antwerp ring and Gardner Museum guards. Others are dead but have close family who can complain, such as Great Train Robbery defendants and the injured train driver's family. A convicted defendant in a famous case has strong 'public interest, newsworthiness' weight. Relatives, bystanders, jurors and acquitted or never-charged people do not. YouTube's process lets the creator 'use the Trim or Blur tools in YouTube Studio' before it reviews, and making the video private does not count as a fix.
findings.action: Show faces only of people central to the documented case: convicted people and officials acting in their role. Blur or leave out relatives, bystanders, witnesses and never-charged suspects. If a privacy complaint comes in, trim or blur the person within the deadline YouTube gives, and never re-upload a removed video with the same people.

findings.topic: Unsolved cases and suspects: defamation, and no ads for 'slander and defamation'
findings.official_quote: Malicious personal attacks, slander, and defamation. (Advertiser-friendly guidelines, 'This content will receive no ad earnings'.) YouTube's Defamation page: "We take into account local legal considerations in our defamation blocking process, and in some cases, we require a court order."
findings.applies: 'D. B. Cooper: What the Files Actually Say' and 'The Gardner Museum Heist' are unsolved. The FBI files name people who were never charged, and some of them or their families are alive. Hatton Garden, the Great Train Robbery and Piltdown are British stories, and YouTube applies 'local legal considerations' when deciding whether to block a video in a country. The kit's promise of 'No guessing about guilt' is exactly the right protection. The risk is breaking it in a script.
findings.action: In unsolved cases, describe named people only as the record does ('the FBI investigated X; X was never charged'), with the source on screen. Never say or suggest guilt beyond a conviction. Keep thumbnails and titles free of an uncharged person's face or name.

findings.topic: Crime documentaries can earn ads; how-to detail and bare CCTV of break-ins earn none
findings.official_quote: Documentaries about crime. (listed under 'This content can earn ad revenue') ... Content meant to educate viewers on how to gain unauthorized access or make unauthorized changes to systems, devices, or property in malicious ways. ... Displaying a house break-in without additional context, e.g. CCTV footage of a house break-in. (listed under 'This content will receive no ad earnings')
findings.applies: Six of the ten titles are heists or thefts. The Mona Lisa script ends 'Next: how he got it out of the building.' Hatton Garden (drilling into a vault) and Antwerp (getting past vault security) invite technical walk-throughs, and the Metropolitan Police published CCTV of the Hatton Garden gang. A history told as a story is in the ad-earning column. A step-by-step method for beating locks, alarms or vaults, or CCTV with no narration, is in the no-ads column. The Community Guidelines also ban 'Instructional theft videos posted with the express intent to steal physical goods or get something for free' (Harmful or dangerous content policy), which a history channel won't do by accident, but it shows where the line is.
findings.action: Tell the method at story level: what happened, why it worked in that year, and how the thieves were caught. Leave out reusable technical specifics such as tool models, alarm defeat steps and vault layouts. Always narrate over CCTV or police footage, and never frame thieves as role models ('genius', 'legend', 'how to').

findings.topic: Violence, injuries and crime-scene images: ad limits, and context must be in the video
findings.official_quote: Content where the focal point is on blood, violence, or injury, when presented without other context, is not suitable for advertising. ... A documentary on a recent homicide featuring descriptive language of the circumstances of death. (limited ad earnings) ... Focus on blood, guts, gore, bodily fluids (human or animal), crime scenes or accident photos with little to no context. (no ad earnings). Violent or graphic content policy: "For educational content containing the kinds of violent or graphic content noted above, this context must appear in the images or audio of the video itself. Providing it in the title or description is insufficient."
findings.applies: Most of the ten titles involve little violence. The exceptions: the Great Train Robbery, where the driver was struck and injured; D. B. Cooper, an air hijacking; and the description's word 'disappearances', which can lead to deaths. YouTube's EDSA page says it 'may not make EDSA exceptions for context that may be in comments, tags, channel descriptions, pinned comments, or other surfaces'. So the kit's good promise of 'no graphic detail for its own sake' protects nothing unless each video's narration carries it. The Harassment policy also bans 'Content reveling in or mocking the death or serious injury of an identifiable individual.'
findings.action: Describe injuries and deaths briefly and without graphic detail. Never put crime-scene, injury or body photos in thumbnails or on screen. Say the who, when, where and why aloud in the narration, and never treat a victim's injury as part of the 'fun' of a heist.

findings.topic: Mugshots, newspaper scans and archive photos: copyright; a credit is not a licence
findings.official_quote: Ultimately, it's your responsibility to verify that a work is in the public domain before you upload it to YouTube. ... For example, works created by U.S. government agencies are automatically in the public domain. (Copyright on YouTube.) Copyright myths: "Giving credit to the copyright owner doesn’t automatically give you the rights to use their copyrighted content."
findings.applies: The description promises 'Sources are listed under every video', which is good for trust, but YouTube says crediting does not give rights. The dispute page also lists 'Giving credit to the copyright owner' among reasons that are 'NOT legitimate reasons to dispute a claim'. FBI material, such as the D. B. Cooper files and sketches, falls under YouTube's 'U.S. government agencies' example. Press photos and news-agency archive images from 1963, 1990, 2003 and 2015, and non-US police photos, are not covered by that line, and their status must be checked one by one. YouTube's own pages say nothing specific about mugshots.
findings.action: Keep a rights log per video: for each image, the source plus why you may use it (public domain with the reason, licence, or own illustration). Where status is unclear, especially news-agency photos and UK police images, use your own illustrations or silhouettes, as the first script already does.

findings.topic: Reused and inauthentic content: scans, slideshows and reading the record aloud
findings.official_quote: Content that exclusively features readings of other materials you did not originally create, like text from websites or news feeds ... Image slideshows, templated storylines, or scrolling text with minimal or no narrative, commentary, or educational value ... Our reused content policy applies to your channel as a whole.
findings.applies: A faceless channel whose visuals are newspaper scans, document pages, text cards and stills is exactly the format these YouTube Partner Program rules describe. 'Told from the record' must not become reading transcripts or articles aloud over scrolling pages. The first script is original narration with its own structure, so it passes. Reviewers also check 'Video metadata (including titles, thumbnails, and descriptions)' and the 'Channel’s “About” section'.
findings.action: Write original narration for every video. Quote records only in short excerpts that you then explain, and vary the visual treatment and story structure between cases. Use the About text to say how each episode is researched and written, so reviewers can see the work is yours.

findings.topic: AI reconstructions and voices of real people
findings.official_quote: Creators must disclose GenAI content that: • Makes a real person appear to say or do something they didn’t do. • Alters footage of a real event or place. • Generates a realistic scene that didn’t actually occur. ... Creators don’t need to disclose non-realistic content that’s made with AI
findings.applies: The script calls for illustrations, silhouettes and text cards. Those are non-realistic, so no disclosure is needed. If later videos use photorealistic AI reconstructions of real people (Peruggia, Lustig, Cooper) or real places, the 'AI use' answer at upload must be Yes. The Harassment policy separately bans 'Content that realistically simulates deceased or abused individuals describing their death or violence experienced', for example an AI voice of an injured guard or driver telling their ordeal.
findings.action: Keep the non-photorealistic illustration style. If any upload includes realistic AI imagery or voices of real people or events, answer Yes under 'AI use' in YouTube Studio. Never give an AI voice to a victim describing what was done to them.

findings.topic: Made for kids
findings.official_quote: General audience content is content that could appeal to everyone, but isn’t intended specifically for children, or content that is intended for a teen or older audience. General audience content should be set as “not made for kids.”
findings.applies: Crime from court records is a teen and adult subject. The illustrated style does not make it child-directed, because YouTube lists 'Animated content that appeals to everyone' as general audience and says it is 'your legal responsibility to comply with COPPA'.
findings.action: Set the channel and every video to 'No, it's not made for kids', and don't use child-oriented characters, songs or keywords in metadata.

review.notes:
No kit wording conflicts with a YouTube rule, so I have no kit_edit. The description's promises ('No guessing about guilt, no graphic detail for its own sake, and respect for the real people involved') match the rules. They only protect a video when the narration itself carries that context, because YouTube does not count channel descriptions as EDSA context. Nothing in the ten titles or the Mona Lisa script breaks a policy. 'Next: how he got it out of the building' is fine as long as that episode stays a story and does not become a technique guide.

Minor, not listed as a finding: 'The Forger Who Fooled the Nazis' can show Nazi-era imagery. The advertiser-friendly guidelines put 'Educational or documentary content: ... Containing focal hate imagery.' under 'This content can earn ad revenue'. The Hate speech policy allows 'Historical footage of an event, like WWII, which doesn't promote violence or hatred' but requires that 'this context must appear in the images or audio of the video itself'. So narrate the context, and avoid a bare swastika as the thumbnail's main image.

YouTube's pages say nothing specific about mugshots. The rules that cover them are privacy, harassment (PII) and copyright, as above. Whether a particular mugshot, UK custody photo or press photo is public domain is a legal question YouTube leaves to the uploader; I did not answer it from memory.

How I read the pages: every quote comes from support.google.com through the reader. The reader drops repeated lines, which removes the ad-earning column labels on the Advertiser-friendly guidelines page. To confirm which column each quoted row sits in, I fetched that same official page once with curl and read the table structure. The quotes themselves are unchanged. The reader also showed an unrelated impersonation paragraph at the top of the violence and harassment pages; I ignored it. I wrote temporary text copies of pages in the scratchpad and deleted them, so no files are left. I did not touch the website repository.

review.audience_setting: Not made for kids: the videos explain deductibles, escrow, leases, liens and contracts for adults, and YouTube's page says "General audience content is content that could appeal to everyone, but isn’t intended specifically for children, or content that is intended for a teen or older audience. General audience content should be set as “not made for kids.”" The simple animated visuals don't change this, because the page also says a video is "not necessarily made for kids just because" it is "safe or appropriate for everyone to watch" and lists "Animated content that appeals to everyone" as general audience.

findings.topic: AI personas on sensitive topics (legal, finance)
findings.official_quote: This policy refers to channels that use AI-generated personas to deliver information on sensitive topics. This includes any content that presents itself as a human expert providing advice to viewers on topics such as health, legal issues, finances, or politics. To protect viewers who may be confused or otherwise negatively impacted by this content, channels uploading this content will not be allowed to monetize. [examples include] AI-generated podcast hosts offering financial guidance, investment tips, or wealth management advice / AI personas giving legal advice or interpreting laws
findings.applies: Every topic on this channel is a legal or money topic under this policy: contracts, leases, liens, insurance and closings. Titles such as "What 'As Is' Means in a Contract" and "How to Read a Lease" interpret legal documents, which is the policy's own example ("interpreting laws"). The kit as written is fine: there is no host, only animated bills, bars and a narrator. The risk is what a faceless channel often adds later, such as an AI presenter, an AI "attorney", "agent" or "broker" character, or two AI podcast hosts. Any of those would make the whole channel ineligible to earn money. This is the one rule that could end monetization for the entire channel, not just one video.
findings.action: Keep the narrator a plain voice, ideally the owner's own voice or a clone of it. Never use an on-screen AI presenter, a named AI character, or an AI host who talks as if they are a lawyer, agent, broker or adviser, and never write lines like "as an attorney" or "in my years as an agent".

findings.topic: Inauthentic (templated) content
findings.official_quote: Generic or repetitive content includes content that looks like it’s made with a template, or that may feel repetitive to viewers after watching several videos in a row from the same channel. ... What’s important is that the substance of each video should be materially varied and deliver creative, educational, or other value.
findings.applies: The kit sets up a fixed format: "Each video explains one term or one document with a simple worked example." The first script uses one sequence of visuals: a bill, two split bars, a seesaw, a calendar, a three-question checklist and a closing title card. The page allows a series ("Same intro and outro for your videos, but the bulk of your content is different"). It refuses "AI-generated content made with generic or unoriginal templates giving the impression of mass production without adding the creator’s original, authentic insights or perspective". Reviewers check the "Main theme", "Newest videos" and the "Channel’s ‘About’ section". So ten videos that all run bill, bars, seesaw, checklist would look interchangeable.
findings.action: Keep only the short open and the closing card the same. Give each video its own worked example and its own visuals: a lease page for leases, a closing table timeline for closings, a lien on a property record for liens. Don't reuse the "three questions to ask" checklist as a fixed segment.

findings.topic: Mass-produced AI videos (Spam policy)
findings.official_quote: Automated or synthetic mass-production: Using automated tools or AI to churn out high volumes of similar content with minimal changes. While testing out new creation tools or posting a few variations of a video is ok, we don't allow use of these tools to flood our platform with repetitive content.
findings.applies: This is a Community Guidelines rule, not just a monetization rule. The page says it can lead to warnings, strikes, suspended monetization or a terminated channel. Its example describes the typical faceless explainer setup: "Channels that use the exact same background music and repetitive AI generated imagery across many videos, with each video reading out an AI-generated script." A glossary channel can produce hundreds of near-identical term videos, which makes it unusually exposed to this rule.
findings.action: Publish at a pace where each script is researched and checked by a person. Vary the music and imagery between videos, and don't batch-generate dozens of term videos from one prompt.

findings.topic: AI disclosure setting ("AI use")
findings.official_quote: Creators don’t need to disclose non-realistic content that’s made with AI, or edits to realistic content that are minor.
findings.applies: The kit's animated bills, bars and seesaw are non-realistic, so they need no disclosure. Narration cloned from the owner's own voice is on the Help page's list of things that need no disclosure ("Cloning one’s own voice to create voice overs or dubs"). A stock AI voice that sounds like a real person is not on either list of the current Help page. However, YouTube's March 18, 2024 blog post (https://blog.youtube/news-and-events/disclosing-ai-generated-content) listed "synthetically generating a person’s voice to narrate a video" as needing disclosure. The same post said "for videos that touch on more sensitive topics — like health, news, elections, or finance — we’ll also show a more prominent label on the video itself." That post is from 2024, and the current Help page describes labels differently. The Help page also says: "Disclosing AI content alone won’t limit a video’s audience or impact its eligibility to earn money."
findings.action: At upload, under Attributes > "AI use": answer No for animated graphics narrated by the owner or the owner's own voice clone. Answer Yes if the narration is a stock AI voice or if any realistic AI imagery is used, such as a photoreal house, office or person.

findings.topic: Sponsorships and affiliate deals in financial services
findings.official_quote: Some categories of branded content come with additional restrictions. To promote goods, services, or brands in these categories, you are responsible for confirming that your brand partners are certified by Google as necessary. You are also responsible to comply with all applicable legal requirements–including using age and country restrictions.
findings.applies: "Financial Services" is on that page's list of restricted categories. This niche will attract offers from mortgage lenders, loan, credit-repair and debt companies, insurers, quote-comparison sites and legal-document services. Google Ads defines financial services as "products and services related to the management or investment of money and cryptocurrencies, including personalized advice" (https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/2464998), and some countries require advertisers to pass "location-specific financial services verification". The branded content page also says any deal "in exchange for payment, free products, or sponsorships (whether you receive the benefit now or later on)" counts, so affiliate commissions very likely count too. A violation "applies to the entirety of your content, not just the portion where the branded content or sponsorship appears."
findings.action: For every sponsored or affiliate video, tick "My video contains paid promotion" in Studio. Before accepting any lender, credit, debt, insurance or investment partner, ask them for proof they are certified or verified by Google for the countries the video reaches, and use the age and country limits that box offers when required.

findings.topic: Quality signals for trust topics (what blogs call YMYL)
findings.official_quote: For quality, our systems are designed to identify signals that can help determine which channels demonstrate expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness on a given topic.
findings.applies: YouTube's own pages never say "YMYL". That label comes from Google Search's rater guidelines, which the reader can't open, so treat "YMYL" as unofficial on YouTube. What YouTube does say is that search weighs expertise, authoritativeness and trustworthiness for every topic. It names extra steps only for "news, politics, medical, and scientific info", not law or finance. It also says evaluators "look at factors like the expertise and reputation of the speaker or channel, the main topic of the video, and whether the content delivers on its promise or achieves its goal." A faceless channel on money and contracts has to earn those signals through accuracy and sourcing, because it can't rely on a credentialed face.
findings.action: Put each video's sources in its description, such as the state insurance department, CFPB or HUD pages or the relevant statute, and pin a correction when something is wrong. Make every title deliver exactly what it promises.

findings.topic: "Required" disclaimers
findings.applies: Only third-party "faceless channel" guides say finance or legal channels must carry a "not advice" disclaimer. None of the YouTube pages read (monetization policies, Spam policy, branded content, AI disclosure, impersonation) requires one, and none says a disclaimer protects a video. The kit already has a good one in the description ("This channel is general education only. It is not legal, insurance or financial advice...") and a spoken one at the end of the script. That fits the AI-persona rule, which targets content that "presents itself as a human expert providing advice". Laws outside YouTube, such as the FTC's sponsorship rules, are separate, and the branded content page says "You and the partners you work with are also responsible for understanding and complying with all applicable legal requirements."
findings.action: Keep the existing disclaimer lines as they are; no change needed. Don't treat them as a shield: what keeps the channel safe is never having a persona that gives advice and never presenting sponsored products as recommendations.

findings.topic: Made for kids
findings.official_quote: General audience content is content that could appeal to everyone, but isn’t intended specifically for children, or content that is intended for a teen or older audience. General audience content should be set as “not made for kids.”
findings.applies: The subjects (deductibles, escrow, leases, liens, closings, life insurance) are for adults. The friendly animated style doesn't make the videos child-directed: the page lists "Animated content that appeals to everyone" as general audience. It also says the creator is legally responsible and should not "rely on our systems to set your audience for you".
findings.action: In Studio > Settings > Channel > Advanced settings, set the channel to "No, set this channel as not made for kids", and confirm "not made for kids" on each upload.

review.notes:
The kit's wording doesn't conflict with any official rule I read, so I have no kit_edit. Its description disclaimer, its \"made-up example\" line and its closing \"not advice about your policy\" card all fit the rules. The one real risk is what gets added later (an AI presenter or AI \"expert\" host), plus a templated look if every video reuses the first script's sequence of visuals.

Outside YouTube's rules, for the fact-check step: the script says a $400 bill is \"under your deductible, so the insurer pays nothing, and there's usually no point in claiming.\" That holds for the car or home repair bill in the example. But the same script then talks about health plans, and the next video covers health-plan terms. On health plans, bills under the deductible usually still count toward it, so the line should stay clearly about car and home policies.

On the coming name change: the impersonation policy (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2801947) bars \"Using a channel name or handle that is phonetically identical or visually similar to an established entity.\" Avoid names close to existing insurers, legal-document sites or real-estate brands, and don't show a real insurer's or agency's logo in a way that suggests a connection.

Not read: Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines, which YouTube links as \"publicly available guidelines\". The reader can't open that host, so the term \"YMYL\" is unconfirmed on YouTube's side.

The 2024 blog line about a more prominent AI label for finance topics may be outdated: the current Help page describes labels by type of content (photorealistic or music), not by topic.

No official YouTube rule requires a licence, a credential check or a disclaimer for legal, insurance or finance explainers. I searched and found only third-party claims.

findings.topic: Generic or repetitive content (the renamed "inauthentic content" rule)
findings.official_quote: What’s important is that the substance of each video should be materially varied and deliver creative, educational, or other value. ... That means channels where content feels interchangeable from video to video are not allowed to monetize. ... Examples of what’s not allowed to monetize (this list is not exhaustive): • Similar or repetitive content with low educational value, commentary, narratives, or minimal variation across videos
findings.applies: Hours-long rain with no voice and a still picture is about as exposed to this rule as a channel can be: the sound is the only thing that can make one video different from the next. The ten titles are different sounds, which is good. But recipe step 5 says to publish every sound twice, as a 3-hour and an 8-hour cut. That makes half the catalogue near-copies of the other half, and that is exactly the "minimal variation across videos" YouTube names. The same page says reviewers focus on a channel's "Main theme", "Most viewed videos", "Newest videos" and "Biggest proportion of watch time". On a channel of 8-hour videos, a few long uploads will hold most of the watch time, so those must be the most clearly original ones. No official page names ambient, sleep or still-image videos as allowed or banned. The test is only whether each video is materially different.
findings.action: Give each sound one length, and make every upload a different recording or mix with its own place, layers and picture. Don't re-upload the same mix at a second length.

kit_edit.quote: 5. Length. Publish one 3-hour and one 8-hour version of each sound.
kit_edit.replace_with: 5. Length. Give each sound one length (3, 8 or 10 hours; YouTube's upload limit is 12). Don't upload the same mix again at another length: two videos of the same sound are interchangeable, and YouTube doesn't monetize channels where videos feel interchangeable.

findings.topic: Reused content: a licence or permission doesn't make it yours
findings.official_quote: Taking someone else’s content, making minimal changes, and calling it your own original work would be a violation of this guideline. If we cannot tell that the content is yours, it may be subject to our reused content policy. This policy applies even if you have permission from the original creator. ... • Content uploaded many times by other creators
findings.applies: Recipe step 1 says that sound "with a licence that allows commercial use on YouTube" is enough. That settles copyright, not YouTube's reused-content rule, which the same page says "is not based on copyright, permission, or fair use." Stock and library rain, including YouTube's own Audio Library effects, is used by many other channels. A video that is mostly one library rain track looped for hours is "Content uploaded many times by other creators", even when licensed.
findings.action: Record the main sound of every video yourself. Use a licensed sound only as one layer in your own mix, never as the whole video, and keep the licence.

kit_edit.quote: 1. Sound. Use rain you record yourself, or sound with a licence that allows commercial use on YouTube. Keep the licence. Sound copied from another channel is what gets these channels demonetized.
kit_edit.replace_with: 1. Sound. Record the main sound of every video yourself. A licensed sound can be one layer in your own mix, never the whole video: a licence settles copyright, but YouTube's reused-content rule applies even with permission, and the same library rain is on many other channels. Keep every licence. Never use sound copied from another channel.

findings.topic: Reused content is judged for the whole channel: show that you made it
findings.official_quote: Our reused content policy applies to your channel as a whole. If you have videos that violate our guidelines, or if we cannot clearly tell that you made the content, monetization may be removed from your entire channel.
findings.applies: With no face and no voice, a reviewer can't see or hear who made the recording. The page says reviewers check the "Channel description", "Video title" and "Video descriptions". It also allows "Reused content from other online sources where the creator is either visible in the content or explains how the creator added to the content". The description is where this channel shows it made the work. Recipe step 7 asks only for the sounds and the loop length, not how they were made.
findings.action: In every video description, say where and how the sound was recorded, what is layered in it and how long the loop is, and credit any licensed layer.

kit_edit.quote: 7. Description. Say what the sounds are and how long the loop is. Don't claim it treats insomnia, anxiety or any condition.
kit_edit.replace_with: 7. Description. Say what the sounds are, where and how you recorded them, what you layered together and how long the loop is, and credit any licensed sound. YouTube's reviewers read descriptions to tell whether you made the content. Don't claim it treats insomnia, anxiety or any condition.

findings.topic: Music and sound licensing: only the Audio Library is known to be copyright-safe
findings.official_quote: Only music and sound effects from the Audio Library are known to YouTube to be copyright-safe. • YouTube is not responsible for issues that arise from “royalty-free” music and sound effects from YouTube channels or other music libraries. ... If you’re using a track with a Creative Commons license, you must credit the artist in your video’s description.
findings.applies: The kit's titles include "Slow Piano and Light Rain for Studying" and the About text lists "a slow piano". Any piano or sound layer that isn't the owner's own recording comes from a library, and YouTube takes no responsibility for claims on "royalty-free" libraries outside the Audio Library. The About text currently says "All sound here is recorded or made for this channel." That stops being true as soon as a licensed layer is used. Also, the same page's reused-content rules bar "Collections of songs from different artists (even if you have their permission)", so the piano can't be a playlist of library tracks.
findings.action: Play or compose the piano yourself, or use one licensed track as a layer. Prefer the YouTube Audio Library for any outside sound, and credit Creative Commons tracks in the description. Make the About text say only what is true.

kit_edit.quote: All sound here is recorded or made for this channel.
kit_edit.replace_with: All sound here is recorded or mixed for this channel. Each video's description says where it was recorded, what is layered in it, and credits any licensed sound.

findings.topic: Phone verification and the 12-hour limit for long uploads
findings.official_quote: By default, you can upload videos that are up to 15 minutes long. Verified accounts can upload videos longer than 15 minutes. ... The maximum file size you can upload is 256 GB or 12 hours, whichever is less. ... If you could previously upload long videos and no longer can, check your account for copyright claims and strikes.
findings.applies: Every planned video is 2 to 10 hours long, so nothing can be uploaded until the account is verified. Longer "12 hours plus" uploads aren't possible. Because the whole channel depends on long uploads, a copyright strike, for example from unlicensed sound, threatens this channel more than most.
findings.action: Verify the account by phone before the first upload, and check that Feature eligibility shows long uploads as enabled. Keep every video under 12 hours, and treat any copyright claim or strike as urgent.

findings.topic: Mid-roll ads on sleep videos
findings.official_quote: By default, automatic mid-roll ad slots are selected for your video. ... While YouTube can automatically suggest the best placement for mid-roll ads, you may want to turn off mid-roll ads if not appropriate. For example, meditation videos may not be suitable for mid-roll ads.
findings.applies: The channel promises "no sudden noises ... so nothing pulls you back". Ads placed automatically through an 8-hour sleep video break that promise, and YouTube itself names meditation videos as a case where mid-rolls may not suit.
findings.action: Once monetized, choose deliberately. Either turn mid-rolls off for sleep videos and keep pre-roll only, or place a few manual slots and switch off automatic slots. Don't leave the default on without deciding.

findings.topic: Content ID can't protect rain and ambient recordings
findings.official_quote: You must have exclusive rights to the material in the reference file for the territories where you claim ownership. The following examples are ineligible for use in or as a reference: • Content licensed non-exclusively from a third party • Content released under Creative Commons or similar free of charge/open licenses ... • Sound effects, soundbeds, or production loops
findings.applies: The channel can't register its rain, wind or noise beds in Content ID, even through a distributor, and licensed or Creative Commons layers can never be registered. Re-uploads by other channels won't be caught automatically. The same rule also means nobody else may properly use a generic soundbed as a Content ID reference.
findings.action: Don't pay a distributor that promises Content ID for ambient sound. Keep your original recording files as proof of ownership, and use the copyright removal form for full re-uploads. If someone claims your own field recording through Content ID, dispute it.

findings.topic: Spam rule: automated mass production
findings.official_quote: Automated or synthetic mass-production: Using automated tools or AI to churn out high volumes of similar content with minimal changes. While testing out new creation tools or posting a few variations of a video is ok, we don't allow use of these tools to flood our platform with repetitive content.
findings.applies: This is a Community Guidelines rule, so breaking it can bring warnings, strikes and termination, not just loss of monetization. The page's own example is "Channels that use the exact same background music and repetitive AI generated imagery across many videos". That is the common way ambient channels are built at volume. A few versions of one sound are allowed; churning out dozens of near-identical rain videos is not.
findings.action: Keep the upload pace to what you can record and mix by hand. Don't batch-generate videos that differ only in title or picture.

findings.topic: AI disclosure for generated music or realistic pictures
findings.official_quote: Creators must disclose GenAI content that: ... • Generates a realistic scene that didn’t actually occur. • Creates music that’s the main focus of the video. ... Note: Disclosing AI content alone won’t limit a video’s audience or impact its eligibility to earn money.
findings.applies: This only applies if AI is used. Examples are an AI-generated piano for "Slow Piano and Light Rain", or a photorealistic AI still of the library, tent or train. The same page warns that creators who "consistently choose not to disclose" may face "suspension from the YouTube Partner Program". Black-screen videos and the owner's own recordings need nothing.
findings.action: If the piano or a photorealistic picture is made with AI, set "AI use" to Yes when uploading. Otherwise set it to No.

review.audience_setting: Not made for kids. Rain and sleep sound is general-audience content, and YouTube says "General audience content should be set as “not made for kids.”" A video is not made for kids just because "It’s safe or appropriate for everyone to watch" or because "Children may incidentally see it." Keep it that way by avoiding lullabies, nursery songs or cartoon characters in titles and pictures (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9528076).
review.notes:
I read every quote above on support.google.com through the reader; all pages loaded and none printed COULD NOT READ.

No official page mentions ambient, sleep, white-noise or still-image/black-screen videos by name. Blogs that say "static image videos are demonetized" or "rain channels can't be monetized" go further than YouTube's words. The official test is the "Generic or Repetitive Content" rule: each video's substance must be materially varied. The closest example, "Image slideshows, templated storylines, or scrolling text with minimal or no narrative, commentary, or educational value", is about slideshows, not a single still under original sound. So the sound has to carry each video's originality.

The monetization policies page now groups the old "repetitious/inauthentic" rule into sections called "Generic or Repetitive Content" and "Unsatisfying or Off-putting Content". The kit's phrase "the inauthentic-content rule" still matches YouTube's July 15, 2025 rename note on that page.

The spam page says "posting a few variations of a video is ok". So the 3-hour/8-hour pairs aren't a Community Guidelines problem, but they are a monetization risk under the generic/repetitive rule.

Distributors' pages (RouteNote, FUGA, Identity Music, Ditto) say nature and white-noise recordings are ineligible for Content ID. That is unofficial, but it agrees with YouTube's official "Sound effects, soundbeds, or production loops" line. TuneCore says otherwise.

Titles must deliver what they say ("8 Hours", "Black Screen"). The spam page's "Malicious clickbait" covers this, but it applies to every channel, so I didn't list it as a finding.

The Copyright Match Tool page (answer/7648743) describes finding re-uploads of your videos. I didn't confirm which channels can use it.

The kit's step 7 line against health claims is consistent with what I read; no change needed.

review.audience_setting: Made for kids, set at the channel level. YouTube says "If your video features actors, characters, activities, games, songs, stories, or other subject matter that reflect an intent to target children, it’s likely made for kids." These wordless picture-book stories, with cute animated snails, pebbles, candles and clouds and a soft marimba, match YouTube's listed factors ("animated characters or cartoon figures", "songs, stories, or poems for children"). Even if adults also watch, YouTube counts mixed-audience content as "a type of made for kids content".

findings.topic: Made for kids (COPPA) audience setting
findings.official_quote: If your video features actors, characters, activities, games, songs, stories, or other subject matter that reflect an intent to target children, it’s likely made for kids. / Whether the video includes characters, celebrities, or toys that appeal to children, including animated characters or cartoon figures. / Mixed audience content, on the other hand, is considered a type of made for kids content.
findings.applies: The channel's characters are cute animated objects and small animals, and the titles read like children's picture books ("The Candle Who Was Afraid of the Dark", "The Little Cloud That Couldn't Rain"). The stories teach simple lessons, like sharing the leaf. That hits several of YouTube's factors. YouTube does list "Animated content that appeals to everyone" as general audience, and "family friendly" alone doesn't make a video made for kids. But that only holds "in the absence of information suggesting an intent to target kids", and here the whole style points at kids. YouTube also says it "may override your audience setting choice in cases of error or abuse", so choosing "not made for kids" would likely be overruled and could bring legal trouble under COPPA.
findings.action: On a computer, open YouTube Studio and go to Settings > Channel > Advanced settings > Audience. Choose "Yes, set this channel as made for kids. I mostly upload content that's made for kids." YouTube says it cannot give legal advice and suggests a lawyer if he is unsure.

findings.topic: What made for kids switches off (ads, comments, bell, memberships)
findings.official_quote: Most importantly, we don’t serve personalized ads on kids content, as required by the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) and/or other applicable laws. Not serving personalized ads on kids content may result in a decrease in revenue for some creators who mark their content as made for kids.
findings.applies: The same page lists features that turn off on made-for-kids videos, including "Comments", "Notification bell", "Personalized advertising", "Save to playlist and Save to watch later", "Channel Memberships" and "Cards or end screens". A channel set as made for kids also loses "Posts". Ads can still run, but only contextual ones: "Contextual ads can be served on YouTube for supervised accounts and on content set as made for kids" (support.google.com/youtube/answer/9713557). So every view earns less, nobody can comment, and the channel can't build a community or get viewer feedback in comments. The script's "END CARD" is fine only as the last frame of the animation itself, not as a YouTube end screen.
findings.action: Plan growth around the Shorts feed and recommendations alone. Don't plan on comments, the bell, playlists, memberships or community Posts, and don't ask viewers to comment or tap the bell. Animate the script's END CARD into the video.

findings.topic: Shorts revenue thresholds from Feb 1, 2027 (Shorts-only, made for kids)
findings.official_quote: To earn each month from the Shorts Creator Pool, creators will now need to maintain 10M qualified Shorts views over the last 90 days. If you miss this threshold, you will not be removed from YPP and this will not impact other YPP earnings, including long-form video. / Starting Feb. 1, 2027, YPP entry thresholds for new creators are changing to 8,000 qualified watch hours in the last 365 days, or 20M qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days, in addition to still needing 1k subscribers.
findings.applies: This channel is more exposed than most, for two reasons. First, it posts only Shorts, so a month under 10M Shorts views in 90 days earns no Shorts ad money at all. Second, it is made for kids, which closes the smaller earning routes: channel memberships require "Channel isn’t set as Made for Kids" and Shopping requires "Channel isn’t set as Made for Kids and doesn’t have a significant number of videos set as made for kids" (support.google.com/youtube/answer/72857). Ads (contextual only) are left as the main income. A new channel joining after Feb 1, 2027 needs 20M Shorts views in 90 days, or 8,000 watch hours. Watch hours from the Shorts feed don't count toward that (support.google.com/youtube/answer/72851). The YouTube Blog (Aug 10, 2026) confirms channels below the Shorts threshold "continue earning on long-form content".
findings.action: Don't build the money plan on Shorts revenue alone. Add longer original episodes (or long videos collecting his own episodes) so the channel can reach the 8,000 watch-hour route and earn watch-page ads. If the channel is in YPP before then, accept the updated terms in YouTube Studio by January 31, 2027.

findings.topic: Inauthentic content: same storyline, same outcome
findings.official_quote: Videos where characters are put in the same situation over and over again with the same outcome (i.e., using a highly similar storyline template across multiple videos) / Similar content, like a series following a set of characters across episodes or a channel that does product reviews, but in which each video has a distinct storyline, focus, or concept / AI-generated content made with generic or unoriginal templates giving the impression of mass production without adding the creator’s original, authentic insights or perspective
findings.applies: The first quote is on YouTube's list of what can't earn money. The second is on its list of what can. The kit's premise is one formula, "tiny characters doing difficult things": a tiny hero meets a huge obstacle, fails, tries again and makes it. The snail script follows that arc, and most of the ten titles invite it (pebble/hill, raindrop/home, ant/crumb, seed/pavement). Ten episodes with the same arc and the same win would match the first quote. YouTube's reviewers look at the "Main theme" and the "Channel’s “About” section", and the current description announces the formula. If AI tools make the animation, the same page allows "using AI to visualize a unique character and narrative you invented", but not templated mass production.
findings.action: Before production, write one line per episode giving its concept and its ending, and make sure no two share the same arc. Vary the endings: some heroes don't make it but find something better, some help another character, some change their minds. Use the description below so it promises varied stories.

kit_edit.quote: Animated shorts about tiny characters doing difficult things: a snail crossing a road, a pebble climbing a hill, a raindrop trying to get home.
kit_edit.replace_with: Animated stories about tiny characters and their big days: a snail who finds a friend at the end of a long road, a candle who is scared of the dark, a paper boat that meets the sea. Every episode is a new story with its own ending.

findings.topic: Inauthentic content: animals in distress or peril
findings.official_quote: Channels that heavily rely on generic templates or emotionally manipulative themes, like a series showing repetitive scenarios of animals in exaggerated distress or peril
findings.applies: This is on YouTube's list of what can't earn money. The heroes are small animals and fragile things (a snail on a road, an ant, a raindrop). The snail script's bicycle-wheel moment is brief and comic, which is fine. The risk is the series sliding into danger as its recurring hook, such as a creature about to be crushed in the opening shot or the thumbnail.
findings.action: Keep danger brief and gentle, and never the main hook. No episode or thumbnail should be built around a creature about to be crushed, drowned or lost. Open on the hero's goal or curiosity instead.

findings.topic: Child safety: death and violence in family cartoons
findings.official_quote: Family friendly cartoons that target young minors and contain adult or age-inappropriate themes such as violence, sex, death, drugs, and more. We don’t allow content labeled as suitable for kids in the video's title, description, tags, or in the audience selection if it contains age-inappropriate themes.
findings.applies: This is a Community Guidelines rule, so breaking it means the video is removed, not just fewer ads. The characters' natural endings are often deaths: a last leaf falling, a candle burning out, a raindrop drying up, a paper boat sinking, a snail under a wheel. With the audience set to made for kids, showing any of those on screen could get a video removed and the channel a strike. Age-appropriate treatment of loss is allowed (YouTube Kids' Preschool setting accepts "loss and grief" handled gently), but on-screen death or injury isn't.
findings.action: No character dies, gets crushed, melts away, burns out or sinks on screen. Give "The Last Leaf Refuses to Fall", "The Candle Who Was Afraid of the Dark" and "A Paper Boat Meets the Sea" gentle endings where the hero changes or finds a new place, not one where it ends.

findings.topic: Quality principles for kids and family content
findings.official_quote: If a channel is found to have a strong focus on low-quality “made for kids” content, it may be suspended from the YouTube Partner Program. / Hard to follow: Videos that are confusing or make no sense, often due to jumbled storylines, unclear audio, or lack of clear storyline (beginning, middle & end). This type of video is often the result of mass production or autogeneration.
findings.applies: Once the channel is made for kids, these principles decide its ad status. YouTube currently enforces six of them (support.google.com/youtube/answer/1311392), and the page says they apply to Shorts. With no words, the pictures alone must carry a clear beginning, middle and end, and AI-stitched clips are the usual way videos become "hard to follow". The snail script passes: it has a clear arc and ends with the snails sharing the leaf, which matches YouTube's high-quality example of "demonstrating kindness, good friendship". One more enforced principle is "Encouraging negative behaviors or attitudes: Content that encourages dangerous activities". YouTube's examples are pranks and unhealthy eating, so a cartoon snail on a road isn't a clear case. Still, a hero setting off across a road with bikes passing could read as unsafe to young viewers.
findings.action: Before uploading, watch each episode without knowing its title. If the beginning, middle and end aren't obvious from the pictures alone, fix it. Optional, at no cost: in the snail script, have it look left, then right before it sets off across the road (2-6s), so it shows a safe habit.

findings.topic: YouTube Kids app
findings.official_quote: Videos set as “made for kids” are not automatically included in the YouTube Kids app.
findings.applies: There is no application; YouTube picks videos "using a mix of automated filters, user feedback, and human review". Gentle wordless shorts suit the Preschool and Younger settings. The Preschool rules (support.google.com/youtube/answer/10938174) ask for "Non-violent and non-scary scripted and animated videos" and say videos there "don’t feature graphic imagery or extreme sadness, anger, or fear". So the bicycle moment, the candle's fear of the dark and the cloud that can't rain need to stay mild. YouTube Kids also excludes branded content, product-focused videos, and misleading, sensational or keyword-stuffed titles and thumbnails. The current titles are plain and fine.
findings.action: Do nothing to apply. Keep fear and sadness mild and resolved within the episode, never put brands or products in episodes, and keep titles and thumbnails as plain as the current ten.

findings.topic: AI disclosure (AI-made animation and music)
findings.official_quote: Creators don’t need to disclose non-realistic content that’s made with AI, or edits to realistic content that are minor. / Using an AI-generated or altered animation of a missile in a fully animated video / Creates music that’s the main focus of the video.
findings.applies: A stylised 3D snail paddling with a flag is clearly not realistic, so AI-made animation needs no disclosure. Two things change that. The page's must-disclose examples include "AI generated music" with no further qualifier, which would cover an AI-made marimba line. A photorealistic real road or real rain could count as "a realistic scene that didn’t actually occur". YouTube adds that "Disclosing AI content alone won’t limit a video’s audience or impact its eligibility to earn money". It may also label videos automatically if its systems detect AI or the file carries C2PA data.
findings.action: At upload, under Attributes > AI use, choose No when the visuals are stylised and the music is made by a person or licensed. Choose Yes if the music is AI-generated or the visuals look photorealistic. Keep the stylised look.

review.notes:
I didn't find any official page saying whether made-for-kids Shorts share in the Shorts feed revenue pool. The Shorts monetization page (12504220) doesn't mention made for kids. The official pages say only that made-for-kids content gets contextual ads, not personalised ones.

Super Thanks has no made-for-kids rule on the official requirements page. It shows in the comments section, though, and comments are off on made-for-kids videos, so it probably won't work here. That is my inference, not an official statement.

The Feb 1, 2027 YPP changes are announced but not yet in force (help page 12843009 and the YouTube Blog post of Aug 10, 2026). The general YPP page (72851) still lists today's 4,000 watch hours or 10M Shorts views.

One URL I guessed, support.google.com/youtube/answer/11089305, printed COULD NOT READ (HTTP 404); I used nothing from it. All quotes above come from pages the reader printed.

Kit inconsistency, not a rule problem: the script's notes say to keep the snail and its flag in every episode, but titles 2-10 star other heroes (a pebble, a raindrop, an ant, a candle...). YouTube allows either a recurring cast or an anthology as long as each video has a distinct story, so the owner should choose one. One option is the snail appearing in each episode beside that episode's hero.

The closing line \"All characters and stories are original to this channel.\" is worth keeping: reviewers read the About section when they check for reused content. None of the ten titles has keyword stuffing or misleading claims.

findings.topic: Phone verification: 2 channels per number per year
findings.official_quote: We use the phone number to send you a verification code. We also make sure the phone number is linked to no more than 2 channels per year. [...] To help prevent abuse, a phone number can only be associated with 2 channels per year.
findings.applies: All ten channels need phone verification. Without it a channel can't post videos longer than 15 minutes or use custom thumbnails. It is also the first step towards monetizing. The same page says: "To access advanced features, you must first complete phone verification. Then, you can choose to build up sufficient channel history or verification using ID or video." The YPP page lists "Have advanced features access on YouTube." as a requirement (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/72851). With one phone number, only two of the ten channels can be verified in a year, so ten would take five years. YouTube's own fix is on https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9891124: "If you've already verified 2 channels with 1 phone number, you must verify a different phone number." No official page says the limit counts per Google Account rather than per channel, so plan for it per channel. With Brand Accounts, only the primary owner can do ID or video verification (same page: "Only primary channel owners can verify their identity to get access to additional features.").
findings.action: Verify the first two channels with your main phone number now. Verify more channels in the same year only with another number you really own and will keep, since it doubles as a recovery number. Never use a borrowed or temporary number. Otherwise wait a year. Check Studio, Settings, Channel, Feature eligibility on each channel before planning uploads that need long videos or custom thumbnails.

kit_edit.quote: • Verify the channel with your phone number (Settings, Channel, Feature eligibility) so you can upload long videos and custom thumbnails.
kit_edit.replace_with: • Verify the channel with your phone number (Settings, Channel, Feature eligibility) so you can upload long videos and custom thumbnails. YouTube lets one phone number verify only 2 channels a year, so verify your first two channels now. Each further channel needs a different phone number you own, or has to wait a year. Every channel needs this step before it can ever be monetized.

findings.topic: A strike or termination on one channel reaches all ten
findings.official_quote: If your YouTube channel is terminated, you are prohibited from using, possessing, or creating any other YouTube channels. You are also prohibited from letting others whose YouTube channels have been terminated use your YouTube channel to bypass their termination. This applies to all of your existing channels, any new channels you create or acquire, and any channels in which you are repeatedly or prominently featured.
findings.applies: One person owns all ten channels, so if one is terminated he loses the right to use the other nine. Termination doesn't always need three strikes: "Sometimes a single case of severe abuse will result in channel termination without warning." (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2802032; the spam policy names spam as one of these). Smaller problems also spread. "Videos with Community Guidelines strikes, copyright strikes, and videos with visuals matching third-party content may contribute to monetization suspension on all your related accounts." (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/1727191). "Violation of our YouTube channel monetization policies may result in monetization being suspended or permanently disabled on all or any of your accounts." (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/1311392). The same page adds: "If any of your channels have been demonetized or terminated, you should not create new (or use existing) channels to get around these restrictions, or apply to YPP with related channels during your suspension period. Doing so could lead to termination of all channels." The kit's wording ("can put the others on the account at risk") is right but understates this.
findings.action: Treat all ten channels as one account at risk. Use only music, footage and sound you made or hold a commercial licence for, and keep the licences. If any channel gets a strike or loses monetization, pause new uploads everywhere, fix or appeal it, and don't apply any other channel to YPP while the suspension lasts. Never open a replacement channel.

kit_edit.quote: Uploading templated videos to ten at once is what YouTube's "inauthentic content" rule removes monetization for, and a serious violation on one channel can put the others on the account at risk.
kit_edit.replace_with: Uploading templated videos to ten at once is what YouTube's "inauthentic content" rule removes monetization for. YouTube's spam policy, which covers "coordinated networks of channels", can also end in termination. Strikes on one channel can cost all your channels their monetization, and if one channel is terminated, YouTube's rules bar you from using any of your other channels.

findings.topic: YPP entry thresholds rise on Feb 1, 2027
findings.official_quote: Starting Feb. 1, 2027, YPP entry thresholds for new creators are changing to 8,000 qualified watch hours in the last 365 days, or 20M qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days, in addition to still needing 1k subscribers. If you are already in YPP, your status is not impacted by this update.
findings.applies: The current numbers on the YPP page are "Get 1,000 subscribers with 4,000 qualified watch hours in the last 12 months, or" "Get 1,000 subscribers with 10 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days." (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/72851). Channels started now (Nov 2026) won't reach those before Feb 1, 2027, so each channel's goal for ad revenue is 1,000 subscribers plus 8,000 watch hours in 365 days, or 20M Shorts views in 90 days. That is double the long-form hours. The lower tier doesn't change and pays fan funding and Shopping, not ad revenue: "Get 500 subscribers with 3 valid public uploads in the last 90 days, and 3,000 qualified watch hours in the last 12 months, or" "Get 500 subscribers with 3 valid public uploads in the last 90 days, and 3 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days" (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/13429240). Each channel qualifies and is reviewed on its own ("Our automated systems and human reviewers will review your channel as a whole", 72851).
findings.action: Update every growth or monetization plan that gives new channels 1,000 subscribers plus 4,000 hours or 10M Shorts views. Use 1,000 subscribers plus 8,000 hours or 20M Shorts views. Treat the 500-subscriber tier as the first milestone, and focus effort on fewer channels so each one can reach 8,000 hours.

findings.topic: AI personas giving advice: official, not just reported
findings.official_quote: This policy refers to channels that use AI-generated personas to deliver information on sensitive topics. This includes any content that presents itself as a human expert providing advice to viewers on topics such as health, legal issues, finances, or politics. To protect viewers who may be confused or otherwise negatively impacted by this content, channels uploading this content will not be allowed to monetize.
findings.applies: The kit's shared notes call this "reported". It is YouTube's own written policy, and it applies to the whole channel, not one video. It covers channel 8 (legal and insurance) and any money channel, such as Stick Ledger's personal finance scripts, if an AI voice or character presents itself as an expert giving advice.
findings.action: Keep finance and legal channels to explaining ideas, without an AI 'expert' character giving advice. Use your own voice or a plainly labelled narrator, and never present the narrator as a lawyer, adviser or doctor.

kit_edit.quote: AI personas giving advice on money, health or law are reported as not monetizable.
kit_edit.replace_with: YouTube's monetization policy says channels whose AI personas present themselves as human experts giving advice on health, legal issues, finances or politics will not be allowed to monetize.

findings.topic: How many channels one Google Account can have
findings.official_quote: You can manage up to 100 channels from one Google Account.
findings.applies: Ten Brand Account channels under one Google Account is well within the limit. YouTube's feature table (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9890437) lists "Add additional channels to your account" as a feature you can't use without verification. Phone verification unlocks it. Creating all ten is allowed, but because of the 2-per-year phone limit, only two can be fully set up (long videos, custom thumbnails, the path to monetization) in the first year on one number. The kit's "Start with three" doesn't fit that limit.
findings.action: Create the ten channels when you like, but launch two first: verify them and upload to them. Add a third only after verifying it with a second phone number you own.

kit_edit.quote: Start with three, not ten. Creating all ten is fine.
kit_edit.replace_with: Start with two, not ten. Creating all ten is fine: one Google Account can manage up to 100 channels. But one phone number can verify only 2 channels a year, so verify and upload to two first.

findings.topic: One AdSense for YouTube account for all channels
findings.official_quote: Important: You can only have one AdSense or AdSense for YouTube account under the same payee name per AdSense Terms and Conditions or AdSense for YouTube Terms of Service, as applicable. Duplicate accounts will not be approved and monetization will be turned off for the associated YouTube channel. [...] You can also monetize more than one YouTube channel using the same AdSense for YouTube account.
findings.applies: All ten channels must be paid through one AdSense for YouTube account in his name, so all ten share one point of failure. On https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/14340193: "Creators disabled for invalid traffic are not allowed any further participation in AdSense. For this reason, these creators may not open new accounts." The same page says "Invalid traffic may affect your channel, even if you're not intentionally driving it." Other limits: "you can only change your linked AdSense for YouTube account once every 32 days". The account must be created in YouTube Studio, not on adsense.com. Monetization pauses if the address PIN isn't verified within 4 months.
findings.action: When the first channel is accepted into YPP, create one AdSense for YouTube account from YouTube Studio's Earn tab and link every later channel to that same account. Never open a second one. Never buy views, subscribers or 'promotion' services on any channel, and never click your own ads. Enter the mailed PIN as soon as it arrives.

findings.topic: 2-Step Verification and one Google Account holding all ten
findings.official_quote: Make sure 2-Step Verification is turned on for your Google Account.
findings.applies: 2-Step Verification on his Google Account is a listed requirement for YPP and for the expanded YPP (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/13429240). All ten Brand Accounts depend on that one Google Account, so a hijack, lockout or deletion affects all of them. https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9367690 says: "Important: If you delete the primary owner account linked to your channel, the channel will also be deleted." YouTube's security page recommends: "For the strongest protection against threats like phishing, set up 2-Step Verification and choose a passkey as your second verification method." (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9701986).
findings.action: Turn on 2-Step Verification with a passkey now, before creating the channels. Add a recovery phone and email, and keep the backup codes on paper. Stay the primary owner of every Brand Account and never delete that Google Account. If anyone helps, give them channel permissions in Studio, never your password.

findings.topic: Similar channels from one owner: spam and inauthentic content
findings.official_quote: This policy applies to all types of content on YouTube, including unlisted and private content, comments, links, posts and thumbnails, and coordinated networks of channels. [...] Automated or synthetic mass-production: Using automated tools or AI to churn out high volumes of similar content with minimal changes. While testing out new creation tools or posting a few variations of a video is ok, we don't allow use of these tools to flood our platform with repetitive content. This includes coordinated mass-production and technical manipulation to bypass filters or trick viewers.
findings.applies: Ten faceless channels from one owner, made with AI voices and templates, is the profile this policy describes. It can lead to strikes and termination, not only lost monetization ("we may suspend your monetization or terminate your channel or account"). Feature access is also delayed or restricted for "Posting the same content repeatedly across one or more channels" and for "Maintaining channels that are related to another policy-violating channel (for example, a repeat spammer or scammer who owns multiple channels)" (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9891124). The monetization policy (updated July 15, 2025, renamed to "inauthentic content") excludes "AI-generated content made with generic or unoriginal templates giving the impression of mass production without adding the creator's original, authentic insights or perspective" (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/1311392). Cross-promotion has limits too: the spam policy lists "Posting identical or similar 'check out my channel' messages across hundreds of videos" and "Using coordinated 'sub-for-sub' schemes."
findings.action: Give each channel its own voice, music, visual style and format, and never upload the same video, or a lightly re-cut copy, to two channels. Cross-promote with a few hand-picked links or playlists, never with copied comments. Grow upload volume only as fast as each video can still be clearly different.

findings.topic: Staying active on every monetized channel
findings.official_quote: Starting February 1, 2027, your channel is considered active if you meet any of the following requirements: 1,000 qualified watch hours in the past 365 days, or 1 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days, or 2 long-form videos or 5 Shorts uploaded every 90 days
findings.applies: Each monetized channel has to stay active on its own. Today's rule is: "we may turn off monetization on channels that haven't uploaded a video or posted to the Posts tab for 6 months or more" (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/72851). Shorts income also has a new floor: "To earn each month from the Shorts Creator Pool, creators will now need to maintain 10M qualified Shorts views over the last 90 days. If you miss this threshold, you will not be removed from YPP and this will not impact other YPP earnings, including long-form video." A small Shorts-led channel can be in YPP and still earn nothing from the Shorts pool.
findings.action: For each monetized channel, plan at least 2 long-form videos or 5 Shorts every 90 days, and never leave one quiet for months. Plan income on long-form ads, and count Shorts-pool money only for a channel already above 10M Shorts views per 90 days.
